meta.blurb: Ines Marlow has the best desk in the tram office, until a humming stranger takes the one opposite. Jonah Pike drinks tea from a chipped blue mug and fixes her printer. Eight weeks, one job, one winner.
meta.bible:
Ines Marlow: a sharp, hard-working tram planner at desk three, proud, tidy, afraid of being ordinary; grew up above a laundry and counted buses from the window; her mother cleaned offices. Jonah Pike: the new planner at desk four, calm, tall, always humming, drinks tea from a chipped blue mug; his grandfather drove trams. Alfie Pike: Jonah's grandfather, 78, retired tram driver of Line 9, gentle and funny. Mrs Faro: the director of planning, fair and watchful. Priya: Ines's friend at desk one, kind and honest. Tomas: the office gossip at desk five. Mr Garrity: a consultant from Garrity and Lowe who offers the Board a cheap plan. Harbourgate: the harbour city. Harbourgate Tram Company: the workplace, second floor, a big window over the harbour. The Clock: the old timetable software. Line 9: the old tram line, closing for good. Line 12: the new line; the prize is the post of Head of Planning for it. Gull Street: a busy crossing. Quay Hill: a steep street. The Board: the group of city leaders who choose; they meet at the Harbour Hall. The task: eight weeks, two plans, one job. Ines's plan is fast trams; Jonah's plan is frequent stops that wait for people. The plan they build together is called fast spine, gentle branches. Ending: Mrs Faro makes two Heads of Planning, Ines and Jonah; they share one desk island, her yellow mug beside his blue one. Voice and tone: warm, quick, funny, gently romantic, a slow-burning rivalry; no bad language, no bad behaviour. Carmen Marlow: Ines's mother, retired, lives on Cable Lane, once cleaned offices at night, phones on Sundays. Bright Laundry: the shop on Cable Lane where Ines grew up in the flat above. Norman: Ines's desk fern. Mina: the cook in the ground-floor canteen, famous for leek soup. Seagate Depot: the tram depot. Harbour Road: the long main road; the fast spine runs along it. The waiting minute: Jonah's idea that a tram waits one minute for anyone running. Mr Hale: the grey-haired chair of the Board. Mrs Adeyemi: a Board member and night nurse who rides the tram. Lantern Square: a tram stop and market. Old Docks: the end of Line 12. The Print Room: the small room with the stubborn printer. The Harbour Wall: the stone wall where Ines eats lunch. Ines's mug: plain white until the end, when she buys a yellow one. Timeline: the contest lasts eight weeks, from a Monday in March; the Board meets on the Friday of week eight.
 Wren Bay: the small town Jonah came from.

beats.scene: Ines walks up a staircase with her coat over her arm, thinking

beats.scene: A woman waits alone at a tram stop in the evening light

beats.scene: Ines at a glowing computer screen in a dark, empty office

beats.summary: Ines finds a small mistake in his figures and circles it in return.

beats.summary: A friendly war of small tricks begins: Ines lowers Jonah's chair as far as it will go.

beats.summary: Next day Jonah moves Norman the fern into the sun, and it perks up.

beats.summary: Ines hides his blue mug, and Jonah makes tea in a jam jar, so she puts it back.

beats.summary: Priya says Ines is enjoying herself; Ines says that is nonsense, but she is smiling.

beats.summary: Ines tells Jonah that she grew up above a laundry and counted buses from the window.

beats.scene: Priya raises her eyebrows at two damp planners entering the office

beats.summary: Jonah suggests they draw the timetables again by hand and fetches a huge roll of paper.

beats.scene: Mrs Faro stands in the doorway of an office watching two laughing planners

beats.scene: Ines sits awake in a tiny flat with a lamp lit at night
beats.summary: At home that night Ines cannot sleep and asks herself why she wants this job so much.

beats.scene: A woman pushes a cleaning cart down a dark office corridor at night
beats.summary: Ines remembers her mother cleaning offices at night with a cart, while little Ines waited.

beats.scene: A small girl sits under a desk in a dark office reading a book
beats.summary: Ines remembers a planner who never looked at her mother, and the promise she made to be somebody.

beats.scene: A narrow shop with a laundry sign and a small window above it
beats.summary: On Sunday Ines visits Carmen at the flat above Bright Laundry on Cable Lane.

beats.scene: Two cups of tea on a table with an older woman smiling kindly
beats.summary: Carmen gives her tea, listens and says that a prize won alone is a lonely prize.

beats.scene: An older woman laughs with her hand over her mouth at a table
beats.summary: Carmen asks about Jonah; Ines calls him her rival, and Carmen laughs.

beats.scene: Ines looks down from an old window at buses passing in the street

beats.summary: On Monday Ines notices that Jonah looks tired too and has been working at weekends.

beats.scene: Jonah holds out a paper train ticket across a desk with a hopeful smile
beats.summary: Jonah invites Ines to ride Line 9 at dawn on Thursday, before it closes the next week.

beats.scene: A paper tram ticket lies on a desk beside an untouched notebook
beats.summary: Ines says no, because she has work to do, and Jonah leaves the ticket on her desk anyway.

beats.scene: Ines stands alone on a tram platform at sunrise
beats.summary: On Thursday before dawn Ines tells herself she will work early, but she walks to the platform instead.

beats.scene: Jonah waits on a misty platform holding two paper cups of tea
beats.summary: Jonah is already waiting with two cups of tea, and he does not look surprised.

beats.scene: An old yellow tram glides into a quiet station as the sky turns pink
beats.summary: The old yellow tram of Line 9 glides in with its lights on as the sky turns pink.

beats.scene: An old man in a blue cap sits on a wooden seat and grins
beats.summary: On the tram sits Jonah's grandfather Alfie in his blue cap, who has come to say goodbye.

beats.scene: A cheerful old man talks and gestures while two young people laugh
beats.summary: Alfie jokes that he was late for everything in his life except this tram.

beats.scene: The tram rolls beside the harbour in golden morning light
beats.summary: The tram rolls along the harbour, and the sun rises over the water.

beats.scene: Alfie raises a finger in the aisle of an empty morning tram
beats.summary: Alfie tells them his driver's rule: never close the doors on someone who is running.

beats.scene: A young woman runs toward a tram while the driver waits at the door
beats.summary: Alfie tells of a night when a woman ran for his tram to reach the hospital in time.

beats.scene: Ines listens with shining eyes while Jonah watches her quietly
beats.summary: Ines listens, moved, and notices that Jonah is watching her instead of the view.

beats.scene: Alfie pats the side of an old tram at the end of the line
beats.summary: At the last stop Alfie pats the tram, says goodbye, and says Harbourgate needs trams that wait for people running.

beats.scene: Ines at her desk staring at a blank page while the office fills
beats.summary: Back at the office Ines cannot work, because Alfie's words keep coming back to her.

beats.scene: Ines walks across the gap between two desks with a nervous face
beats.summary: Ines crosses the gap between the desks and asks Jonah if she may use his waiting-minute idea.

beats.scene: Jonah looks up surprised, then pleased, from behind a blue mug
beats.summary: Jonah looks surprised and then pleased and tells her to take it, because an idea is only good when it is used.

beats.scene: Ines holds out a hand across two desks in a quiet office
beats.summary: Ines proposes a fair fight with no more tricks, and Jonah agrees at once.

beats.scene: Two hands clasped over two desks while colleagues watch quietly
beats.summary: They shake hands on it, and the handshake lasts a little too long.

beats.scene: A calendar with two weeks left circled in red beside a pile of maps
beats.summary: The Board meeting is two weeks away, and both planners begin to work late nights again.

beats.scene: Two open boxes of noodles among papers on a Print Room table
beats.summary: They eat takeaway noodles in the Print Room and argue happily about chopsticks.

beats.scene: Two people lean over a stopwatch and a timetable under a lamp
beats.summary: They test timings with a stopwatch, and Jonah hums while Ines no longer minds.

beats.scene: Priya whispers to Tomas behind a computer screen, pointing
beats.summary: Priya tells Ines that she has started to hum, and Ines denies it.

beats.scene: Ines glances up from her work as a door opens with a soft sound
beats.summary: Ines notices that she looks up every time Jonah comes in, and tells herself it means nothing.

beats.scene: Dark storm clouds roll over a grey harbour past an office window
beats.summary: A storm warning arrives on Friday in week six, and the sky over the harbour turns dark.

beats.scene: The office empties as people hurry out in coats while two stay
beats.summary: Everyone goes home early, but Ines and Jonah stay to finish their drafts.

beats.scene: A bright flash of lightning outlines a window above a harbour
beats.summary: A great flash of lightning lights the harbour, and the thunder comes at once.

beats.scene: A dark office with every light out and a dim window
beats.summary: The power goes out, and the whole office, and the city outside, falls into darkness.

beats.scene: Two phone lights glow on the floor beside a big dark window
beats.summary: They sit on the floor by the window, lit by the glow of two phones.

beats.scene: Two faces lit softly by phone light talk in a dark room
beats.summary: In the dark Jonah admits he is afraid of losing, because he cannot bear to disappoint Alfie.

beats.scene: A woman's face turned toward the dark window and the rain
beats.summary: Ines admits that she is afraid of being ordinary, of being no one special at the end.

beats.scene: Two people sit close together on a floor with a rain-streaked window
beats.summary: Jonah tells her she is not ordinary, and she laughs, and their hands are very near.

beats.scene: Two faces very close together in dim glow before a rainy window
beats.summary: They lean toward each other in the dark, and they almost kiss.

beats.scene: Office lights flicker on over two people springing apart on the floor
beats.summary: The lights come back with a sudden hum, and they step apart as if they had been caught.

beats.scene: Ines sits very straight at her desk, avoiding the empty chair opposite
beats.summary: On Monday Ines arrives early, keeps her eyes on her screen and avoids looking at Jonah.

beats.scene: Jonah carries a laptop and a mug to a far table of the office
beats.summary: Jonah, who has understood, takes his laptop to a far table at the other end of the room.

beats.scene: Priya watches two empty-looking desks and a lonely fern
beats.summary: Priya sees how far apart they now sit and how little they speak.

beats.scene: Priya and Ines sit on the harbour wall with untouched sandwiches
beats.summary: At lunch Priya asks what happened, and Ines says nothing did, and Priya tells her to be honest with herself.

beats.scene: Mrs Faro speaks gravely to two planners across a meeting table
beats.summary: Mrs Faro calls them both in: the Board is nervous, and a firm of consultants has offered a cheaper plan.

beats.scene: A tall man in a smooth grey suit shakes hands in a busy office
beats.summary: Mr Garrity of Garrity and Lowe visits the office in a smooth grey suit and smiles at everyone.

beats.summary: Mr Garrity shows his plan: cut the stops, cut the staff and save money, with trams running only along the main road.

beats.summary: Jonah says politely that a plan which leaves out the people who run is not a plan for the city.

beats.summary: Mrs Faro says the Board will watch a real test on Saturday: Ines's plan and Jonah's plan, each on one stretch.

beats.scene: Ines and Jonah study a route map at two separate tables at dusk
beats.summary: They prepare for the test separately and awkwardly, and neither knows how to speak to the other.

beats.scene: Board members in coats with notebooks stand at a sunny tram stop
beats.summary: On Saturday morning the Board gathers at Lantern Square with notebooks, in clear cold light.

beats.summary: Ines's test begins: the fast trams glide along her stretch with few stops, exactly on time.

beats.summary: Ines sees the woman left behind, and her stomach drops as the Board members write notes.

beats.summary: Mrs Adeyemi, the night nurse, tells Ines quietly that she often runs for trams after her shift.

beats.summary: The Board goes off for coffee, and Mr Hale gives no sign of what he thinks.

beats.summary: Ines and Jonah stand by the empty track and neither speaks; at last Jonah suggests a walk.

A1A2: Ines Marlow loved her desk by the big window at the Harbourgate Tram Company.
Ines put her white cup, her fern and her pencils in the same places every day.
From her window, Ines counted the trams as they crossed Gull Street.
Priya came in with two coffees and said the office had news.
Tomas said a new planner was coming and would sit opposite Ines.
At lunch, Mina gave them hot soup, and everyone talked about the new man.
Back at her desk, Ines worked on a timetable with the old Clock program.
Mrs Faro said the new planner was good and hoped Ines would be kind.
Ines had to clear her maps from the empty desk across from hers.
On Sunday, Ines called her mother, who said she should be kind.
On Monday, Mrs Faro brought a tall stranger to the empty desk.
Jonah held out his hand, and Ines shook it quickly.
Jonah took out a blue mug with a chip and began to hum.
Ines put her tall pencil case between them like a small wall.
Tomas showed Jonah around, and soon everyone liked the new man.
At lunch on the Harbour Wall, Ines said Jonah was too cheerful.
Priya said Ines was unfair, but Ines did not trust easy people.
In the afternoon, Jonah asked Ines how to use the Clock.
At five o'clock, Jonah put on his coat and left, humming.
Ines saw Jonah's paper covered with small marks counting trams.
On Tuesday, Mrs Faro called everyone together and held up a folder.
Mrs Faro said Line 9 would close, and a new Line 12 would open.
The new line needed one Head of Planning, and there was only one job.
Mrs Faro said two planners would each write a plan for Line 12.
The contest would last eight weeks, ending with a Board meeting.
Jonah smiled and said, may the best plan win.
Ines asked Mrs Faro why a new man could compete for the job.
Ines told Priya she would win, and Priya said she worked too hard.
Ines began her plan with a straight line and very few stops.
Across the room, Jonah drew a map with many small stops.
The old printer in the Print Room jammed again on Ines.
Ines pulled out the torn paper, but it jammed a third time.
Jonah came to the door with a tool and asked to try.
Ten minutes later, Jonah held up a tiny piece of pencil.
Jonah printed her pages first and gave them to her.
Tomas told the whole office about the printer within the hour.
Priya said Jonah was a gift, but Ines said he was a threat.
Ines worked late every evening, but Jonah left at five.
One night, Ines ate cold noodles alone and watched the harbour lights.
On Friday, Jonah offered Ines a pastry, but she said no.
Both planners chose Wednesday morning to measure Gull Street.
Ines arrived at six with her watch and notebook, and Jonah was already there.
They bumped into each other, and papers flew across the road.
They counted riders from different corners, but their numbers did not match.
Jonah talked to people at the stop, but Ines only counted.
At the office, they argued over a map about fast trams or many stops.
Their voices grew louder, and Tomas hid behind his screen.
Mrs Faro heard both ideas and said both were good.
Ines was angry at herself, but Jonah said it was a good argument.
On the tram home, Ines remembered something a woman had said.
Late one night, Ines opened Jonah's plan on the shared computer.
Jonah's plan was clear and kind, and it was very good.
Ines felt guilty for looking, and she was also afraid.
Next morning, Ines found a yellow note on her map with a circled mistake.
Ines found a small mistake in his figures and circled it too.
Jonah thanked her for the mistake, which annoyed her even more.
A small war began, and Ines lowered Jonah's chair.
The next day, Jonah moved Norman the fern into the sun.
Ines hid Jonah's blue mug, so he drank tea from a jam jar.
Priya said Ines was enjoying herself, and Ines said it was nonsense.
In the fourth week, heavy rain stopped the trams at Gull Street.
Mrs Faro sent Ines and Jonah out to fix the schedule.
They rode a crowded tram, and Ines stood close to Jonah.
Jonah said his grandfather drove Line 9 for forty years.
Jonah's grandfather Alfie was seventy-eight and sad that Line 9 was closing.
Ines told Jonah she grew up above a laundry and counted buses.
The tram stopped in the flood, and the passengers began to worry.
Together they found a new route through Lantern Square, and it worked.
Soaked and cold, they drank hot tea at a stall, and Ines laughed.
At the office, Priya noticed they both had wet hair and bright eyes.
On Wednesday, the Clock crashed, and the screen turned blue.
Both planners lost a day of work, and both turned pale.
Tomas said the computer man was on holiday and there was no copy.
Jonah said they should draw it all by hand and got a big roll of paper.
They sat on the floor and drew the timetables by hand.
At six, they shared a sandwich, and Mina sent up soup.
They both found the same problem: Quay Hill was too steep.
They saw that neither plan could solve Quay Hill alone.
At midnight they finished and laughed because they were so tired.
In the morning, Mrs Faro saw them laughing and reminded them only one could win.
That night at home, Ines could not sleep and asked why she wanted to win.
Ines remembered her mother cleaning offices at night with a big cart.
Ines remembered a promise she made as a child in an office.
On Sunday, Ines visited her mother's flat above Bright Laundry.
Carmen gave Ines tea and said that a prize won alone is lonely.
Carmen asked about Jonah, and Ines called him her rival.
Before she left, Ines looked from her old window and counted buses.
On Monday, Ines saw that Jonah looked as tired as she did.
Jonah invited Ines to ride Line 9 at dawn on Thursday.
Ines said no, but Jonah left the ticket on her desk.
Before dawn on Thursday, Ines went to the platform after all.
Jonah was waiting with two cups of tea and did not look surprised.
The old yellow tram came in slowly as the sky turned pink.
On the tram sat Alfie, Jonah's grandfather, wearing a blue cap.
Alfie joked that he was late for everything except this tram.
The tram rolled along the harbour while the sun came up.
Alfie told them his rule: never close the doors on someone running.
Alfie told a story about a woman who ran for his tram one night.
Ines was moved by the story and saw Jonah watching her.
At the last stop, Alfie said goodbye and said trams should wait for people running.
Back at the office, Ines could not work because of Alfie's words.
Ines walked to Jonah's desk and asked to use his waiting minute.
Jonah looked surprised and then pleased and told her to take it.
Ines asked for a fair fight with no more tricks, and Jonah agreed.
They shook hands on it, and the handshake lasted too long.
The Board meeting was two weeks away, and they worked very hard.
They ate noodles in the Print Room, and Jonah dropped most of his.
They tested the timings by watch, and Ines no longer minded his humming.
Priya told Ines she had started to hum, but Ines denied it.
Ines noticed she looked up every time Jonah came in.
On Friday, a storm warning came, and the sky turned dark.
Everyone went home early, but Ines and Jonah stayed to finish.
A great flash of lightning lit the harbour, and thunder followed.
Then the power went out, and the whole city went dark.
They sat on the floor by the window with two small phone lights.
In the dark, Jonah said he was afraid of losing for Alfie's sake.
Ines said she was afraid of being ordinary.
Jonah said she was not ordinary, and their hands were very near.
They leaned closer in the dark, and they almost kissed.
The lights came back, and they jumped apart.
On Monday, Ines kept her eyes on her screen and did not look at Jonah.
Jonah understood and took his laptop to a table far away.
Priya saw how far apart they sat and how little they spoke.
At lunch, Priya asked what happened, and Ines said nothing.
Mrs Faro told them the Board was nervous about a cheaper plan.
Mr Garrity visited the office in a smooth grey suit.
Mr Garrity showed his plan: fewer stops, fewer staff and less money.
Jonah said politely that a plan without people was not a plan.
Mrs Faro said the Board would see a real test on Saturday.
They prepared for the test separately, and it felt strange.
On Saturday morning, the Board gathered at Lantern Square with notebooks.
Ines's test began, and the fast trams ran exactly on time.
Ines felt proud as the Board nodded, and a crowd gathered at the stop.
A woman with a baby ran for the tram, but the doors closed.
Ines saw the woman standing alone, and she felt sick.
Mrs Adeyemi told Ines that she often ran for trams after work.
Jonah's test began, and a boy with a bag ran and reached the tram.
But the trams filled up, and all the stops made them slow.
A driver said on the radio that he could not keep to time.
The Board went for coffee, and Mr Hale gave no sign.
Ines and Jonah stood by the empty track, and Jonah asked, Walk?
At dusk, they sat on the Harbour Wall, and the water was quiet.
Ines said honestly that her plan left a woman behind.
Jonah said his plan made the line crawl.
They both said they were wrong, and then they laughed.
They agreed the woman with the baby was the most important person.
Ines drew a long straight line with small branches on paper.
Jonah stared at her drawing and said it was the answer.
They both wanted to give the idea to the other, and they laughed.
They decided to join their plans, and they ran back to work.
That night, two lamps burned late as they began the joint plan.
They drew the fast spine along Harbour Road with five big stops.
Then Jonah drew gentle branches to Lantern Square, Cable Lane and Quay Hill.
They shared the work: Ines did the timings and Jonah did the stops.
Ines solved Quay Hill with the light new trams and a short branch.
At three in the morning, Jonah poured tea and offered the blue mug.
At last, the Clock accepted the whole timetable, and they saved it five times.
At sunrise, they fell asleep in their chairs, then walked home.
On Monday, Mrs Faro read the joint plan on the wall and smiled.
Mrs Faro said there were five days left and only one post.
On Thursday evening, Ines saw Jonah talking on the phone by the window.
She heard him say, Yes, Mr Garrity, I will think about it.
Ines slipped away with her mind racing about the offer.
She lay awake all night, and old fears came back.
On Friday morning, Jonah brought two coffees, but Ines said nothing.
In front of everyone, Ines said she had heard his phone call.
Jonah said he turned the offer down, but Ines did not listen.
Tomas and Priya stared, and Priya tried to speak, but could not.
Jonah said he thought they were past this, and he took his mug.
Ines took her coat and walked out of the building alone.
Ines sat alone on a cold bench on the quay while gulls flew.
She told herself she was right to be careful, but she felt sick.
She remembered all of Jonah's small kindnesses, one after another.
An old man in a blue cap sat down beside her on the bench.
Alfie said Jonah had turned down Mr Garrity's offer.
Alfie explained the offer: a high job if Jonah gave up the contest.
Alfie said Jonah refused because he would not leave someone behind.
Ines said she had not let Jonah finish, and Alfie said trams wait.
Ines thanked Alfie, hugged him and ran back toward the office.
At the office, Ines found desk four empty and the plan on her desk.
The note said Jonah had gone to the Harbour Hall with the plan.
Ines grabbed the plan and ran down the stairs while Priya shouted.
Rain began to pour, and the tram for the Harbour Hall was leaving.
The driver saw her running and stopped the tram for her.
The driver said Alfie had told him someone might come running.
The tram rolled through the rain while Ines watched the time.
At the Harbour Hall, she jumped off and ran up the stone steps.
A guard tried to stop her, but let her in when she gave her name.
Inside, Jonah stood alone before the Board beside an empty chair.
Ines walked in, wet and tired, and sat in the empty chair.
Ines and Jonah gave the plan together: Ines the numbers, Jonah the people.
Mr Garrity said the joint plan was too soft, and Ines answered.
Mrs Adeyemi asked about the waiting minute, and Jonah explained it.
In the corridor, Ines said sorry, and Jonah said the tram was running.
The Board returned and Mr Hale said they preferred the joint plan.
Mrs Faro held up two letters: both planners were Head of Planning.
Weeks later, Alfie drove the first test tram, and Ines and Jonah kissed.
Ines bought a bright yellow mug at the depot shop.
Six months later, the first Line 12 tram waited for a running girl.
Back at the office, the two desks stood together, with two mugs.
B1B2: Every morning, Ines Marlow arrived before anyone else and watched the harbour wake up from her desk. She had worked at the Harbourgate Tram Company for six years, and she knew every timetable by heart.
Her desk was always tidy, with a white cup on the left and eight sharp pencils in a neat row. A small fern called Norman sat by the window, and she watered him every morning.

She had counted vehicles from windows since she was a small girl, and she still did it without thinking. Below her, the first trams of the morning rolled across Gull Street, and she knew each one by its time.
Priya, who sat at desk one, arrived at half past eight with two paper cups of coffee. She put one beside Ines's white cup and said that everyone downstairs was talking about something.
Tomas, the office gossip at desk five, said that a new planner was starting on Monday. He added, with a wide smile, that the man would have the empty desk right opposite Ines.
At lunch, Mina the cook filled their bowls with her famous leek soup. Everybody at the long table wanted to guess who the new planner would be and where he had come from.

The Clock was the old software that made every timetable in the company, and it was slow and rather stubborn. Ines had learned to work around its moods, and she was proud of every plan that survived it.
Mrs Faro, the director of planning, stopped beside Ines's desk before she went home. She said the new planner was very good and that she hoped the two of them would get along.
For a whole year, Ines had used the empty desk opposite as a place for her maps. On Friday afternoon she gathered them up with a sigh and wiped the empty surface clean.
On Sunday evening Ines phoned her mother, Carmen, as she always did. Carmen listened to the story about the new planner and said that a kind word costs nothing.
On Monday morning the director, Mrs Faro, walked in with a tall stranger and pointed at the empty desk across from Ines. His name was Jonah Pike, and he was the new planner.
Jonah leaned across the two desks and held out his hand with a friendly smile. Ines shook it quickly and told him that the window was on her side of the room.
Jonah unpacked his things slowly, and the last thing out of the box was a blue mug with a chip in its rim. He filled it with tea and hummed a tune that went nowhere in particular.
Ines tried to ignore the humming and finally stood her pencil case on the edge of the desk like a wall. Jonah noticed it at once and, to her annoyance, did not seem offended.
Tomas took Jonah around the floor and introduced him to everyone. Jonah remembered every name after hearing it once, and within an hour half the office was laughing at his jokes.
At lunch Ines and Priya sat on the Harbour Wall with their sandwiches and watched the gulls. Ines said that nobody could really be that cheerful all day, and that it simply had to be an act.
Priya told her gently that she was being unfair, since the man had only said hello. Ines replied that she never trusted people who made everything look so easy, because in her experience nothing was.
In the afternoon Jonah asked Ines how to make the Clock save a timetable properly. She gave him a short answer, and he thanked her so warmly that she felt strangely suspicious.

At exactly five o'clock Jonah put on his coat, said goodnight to the whole room and walked down the stairs humming. Ines stayed where she was, and she told herself that serious planners never left on time.
As she tidied up that evening, Ines glanced at the paper on Jonah's desk. It was full of small pencil marks in rows of five, and he had clearly been counting trams.
On Tuesday morning Mrs Faro asked everyone to stop work and stand in front of her. She held a thin grey folder in both hands and waited until the room was perfectly quiet.
She told them that old Line 9 would close for good in eight weeks. In its place, the city would build a new, modern tramline called Line 12.
A new line, she said, needed a Head of Planning, and there would be only one such post. Everyone in the room understood at once that this was the biggest job in the company.
She explained that two planners would each write a complete plan for Line 12, and that the Board would choose the better one. Those two planners, she said, were Ines Marlow and Jonah Pike.
The contest would last eight weeks, she said, and it would end on a Friday when the Board met at the Harbour Hall. Until then, both planners had the same time, the same tools and the same rules.
Jonah turned to Ines and said, quite calmly, that he hoped the best plan would win. Ines found it very strange that anyone could say those words and mean them.
After the meeting Ines went into Mrs Faro's office and asked why a newcomer should be allowed to compete. Mrs Faro answered that the Board wanted fresh eyes, and that Jonah was a very good planner.
At lunch Ines told Priya, in a very firm voice, that she was going to win the job. Priya answered that she already worked too hard, and she asked whether Ines ever planned to rest.
That evening Ines began her plan with a long straight line from Quay Hill to the Old Docks. She wanted fast trams and very few stops, so that a person could cross the city in twenty minutes.

Across from her, Jonah was drawing a very different map, with many small stops and little notes beside each one. At one of them he had written two words that she could just read upside down, the waiting minute.
The old printer in the Print Room had been jamming for weeks, and it chose the worst moment to do it again. Ines needed her first pages for Mrs Faro by ten o'clock, and the machine only groaned.
Ines pulled out the crumpled sheets and tried again, but the printer jammed for a third time. She stood there with her hands on her hips and a small, hot feeling behind her eyes.
Jonah appeared in the doorway of the Print Room with a small screwdriver in his hand. He asked politely if he might try, and before Ines could say no, he was kneeling beside the machine.
In ten minutes he found the problem, and it was a tiny stub of pencil stuck in a roller. He held it up with a grin and said that someone must have dropped it years ago.
Once the printer worked again, Jonah printed Ines's pages before his own and handed them to her with a small bow. She said thank you in a voice as cold as the harbour in winter.
By lunchtime Tomas had told the entire floor how the new man fixed the printer in ten minutes. Several people clapped Jonah on the back, and Ines pretended to be very busy.
Priya told Ines in the stairwell that Jonah was a gift to the whole office. Ines said he was not a gift but a threat, and that kind people were the most dangerous of all.
All that week Ines worked until nine o'clock every night, and Jonah left at five to walk by the harbour. He told her, quite cheerfully, that tired minds make bad timetables.
One night she ate cold noodles at her desk and looked out at the harbour lights. The office was so quiet that she could hear the clock tick, and she felt, for a moment, a little lonely.
On Friday Jonah arrived with two pastries from the bakery on Cable Lane and offered one to Ines. She refused it politely, and Tomas, who had been watching, ate it with great pleasure.
In the second week Mrs Faro asked both planners to measure the crossing at Gull Street. Without telling each other, they both chose Wednesday at dawn, when the first workers ride to town.
Ines reached Gull Street at six o'clock with her stopwatch and her best clipboard. Jonah was already there, leaning on a lamp post with a flask of tea, and he waved as if he were happy to see her.
They both stepped forward to start counting at the same moment, and their clipboards knocked together. Papers flew across the road, and they spent a full minute running after them between the cars.
They stood on opposite corners and counted every rider who stepped off a tram. When they compared their sheets afterwards, the totals were far apart, and neither of them wanted to admit a mistake.
While Ines counted, Jonah talked with the people waiting at the stop and asked them why they were always late. Ines told him that numbers were facts and stories were only stories.
Back at the office they spread a big map across the table and began to argue. Ines wanted fast trams with few stops, while Jonah wanted frequent stops and trams that waited for people.
Their voices got louder and louder, until Tomas slid down behind his computer screen. Priya, at desk one, raised one eyebrow as high as it would go.
Mrs Faro came in, listened to both ideas without a word and then said that both were good. When Ines asked which was better, she only smiled and said that was the Board's question.
Afterwards Ines was angry with herself for losing her temper in front of everyone. On the stairs Jonah told her that the argument had been the best part of his week, and she did not know what to say.
On the tram that evening Ines remembered one of the notes Jonah had shown her. A woman at the stop had said that she did not need a fast tram, only one that was still there when she arrived.
One night in the third week, Ines was working alone when she noticed Jonah's folder on the shared server. She told herself that she would only look at the title, and then she opened it.
His plan was clear and careful, and every stop had notes about the real people who would use it. At each one he had written the waiting minute, a short pause for anyone who was running.
She felt guilty about looking at his work without asking. Underneath the guilt was something worse, a cold little fear that Jonah might really be better than she was.
The next morning there was a yellow note stuck on Ines's map, and a pencil circle drew her eyes to a tiny error. It was a wrong angle on a curve at Lantern Square, and Jonah was right.

Ines hid Jonah's blue mug in a cupboard, and at tea time he made his tea in an old jam jar. He seemed perfectly happy, and she felt so guilty that she put the mug back before lunch.

In the fourth week a storm of heavy rain flooded the junction at Gull Street. By nine o'clock the trams had stopped, and the whole city seemed to be late.

Ines surprised herself by telling Jonah that she had grown up in a flat above a laundry on Cable Lane. As a child she had counted the buses from the window, and that was how she first fell in love with timetables.

Carmen asked what kind of man Jonah was, and Ines called him her rival. Carmen laughed so hard that she had to put down her cup, and she would not say why.
Before she left, Ines stood at her old window above the street and counted the buses. There were fewer than there had been when she was a girl, and the street seemed quieter.
On Monday morning Ines noticed that Jonah looked just as tired as she did. His hair was untidy and there were dark rings under his eyes, and she realised he had been working at weekends as well.

Ines told him that she had too much work and could not possibly go. Jonah only nodded and left the ticket on her desk, and then he went back to his own.

On Thursday, long before dawn, Ines told herself she was going to the office early. Instead her feet carried her to the old tram platform, and she stood there in the cold with the ticket in her pocket.
Jonah was already there, holding two paper cups of tea in the grey light. He did not seem surprised to see her, and he handed her a cup as if he had known all along.
Then the old yellow tram of Line 9 slid into the station with its lights on. The sky behind it was turning pink, and the whole street looked as though it were holding its breath.
On the tram, in the very first seat, sat an old man in a blue cap. This was Alfie, Jonah's grandfather, and he had come to say goodbye to his tram.
Alfie told them that he had been late for his wedding, his own birthday and most funerals. But in forty years he had never once been late for this tram.
The tram rolled slowly along the harbour while the sun rose over the water. The ships and the cranes turned gold, and for a moment nobody said anything at all.
Alfie told them the one rule that he had kept for forty years. He never closed the doors of the tram while someone was still running toward it.
One night, Alfie said, a young woman had run for his tram with a small suitcase in her hand. He had waited for her, and she had reached the hospital in time for her baby to be born.
Ines listened with shining eyes and a lump in her throat. When she turned her head, she found that Jonah was watching her face and not the view.
At the last stop at the Old Docks, Alfie patted the side of the tram like an old horse. He said that Harbourgate did not need faster trams, only trams that waited for people who were running.
Back at the office Ines sat in front of a blank page for an hour. Alfie's words about people who run kept coming back to her, and she could not push them away.
Ines stood up, crossed the little gap between their desks and swallowed her pride. She asked whether she might use his idea of a waiting minute in her own plan.
Jonah looked surprised, then pleased, and then he told her to take it. A good idea, he said, only does good when somebody uses it.
Ines then said that from now on the contest should be fair, with no more tricks or hidden mugs. Jonah agreed at once, and he said that he had never really enjoyed the chair.
They shook hands across the two desks to seal the agreement. The handshake went on a little longer than it should have, and the whole office was suddenly very quiet.
Now the Board meeting was only two weeks away, and both planners began to work late again. This time the work felt different, because they no longer worked in secret.
They ate takeaway noodles in the Print Room one night, surrounded by maps. Jonah could not use chopsticks at all, and Ines showed him how with a pair of pencils.
They tested the timings of the new line with a watch, one stop at a time. Jonah hummed while he counted, and Ines noticed that she did not mind it any more.
Priya told Ines at lunch that she had started humming at her desk. Ines said that this was ridiculous, and then she realised that she was humming right then.
Ines realised that she looked up every time the office door opened, and she knew exactly who she was hoping to see. She told herself it meant nothing, and she did not believe it.
On Friday afternoon a storm warning was announced, and the sky over the harbour grew darker by the minute. The sea turned the colour of iron, and the gulls disappeared.
Everyone else hurried home before the storm could break over the city. Ines and Jonah stayed behind, because each of them wanted to finish a draft before the weekend.
A great flash of lightning lit up the whole harbour, and the thunder came at once. The windows rattled, and the lamps on the desks flickered like candles.
Then every light in the office went out at the same moment. Outside, the streets and the harbour were dark too, and the whole city had disappeared into the night.
They carried two phones to the floor by the window and sat down with their backs against the wall. The tiny lights made two small circles, and the rain beat steadily on the glass.
In the dark, honesty came more easily, and Jonah said that he was afraid of losing. It was not for himself, he explained, but because he did not want to let his grandfather down.
Ines surprised herself again and said that her own fear was being ordinary. She was afraid that, after all her work, she would turn out to be no one special at all.
Jonah said that she was the least ordinary person he had ever met. Ines laughed, but it was a shaky laugh, and she noticed that their hands were lying very close together on the carpet.
Slowly they leaned toward each other in the dark until their faces were only a few centimetres apart. Ines could hear her own heart, and she thought that Jonah could hear it too.
Then the lights came back on with a loud hum, and the computers began to beep. They jumped apart like two children caught stealing biscuits, and both of them started to talk about the Clock.
On Monday morning Ines arrived early and kept her eyes fixed on her screen. She did not look at Jonah once, and she answered his friendly good morning with a nod.
Jonah seemed to understand without needing to be told anything at all. He picked up his laptop and his mug and moved to an empty table at the far end of the room.
Priya noticed that the two planners had stopped talking to each other altogether. Even Tomas, who loved a quarrel, said that this was not a happy quiet.
At lunch Priya asked her directly what had happened on the night of the storm. Ines said that nothing had happened, and Priya told her gently that she should be honest with herself.
Mrs Faro called them into her office and said that the Board was getting nervous. A firm of consultants had offered a cheap plan of their own, and some members liked the price.

The next day Mr Garrity, from the firm of Garrity and Lowe, visited the office in a smooth grey suit. He smiled at everyone, shook every hand and looked around the room as if he were thinking about buying it.
Mr Garrity showed the planners his own plan on a bright screen. He wanted to cut the number of stops and the number of staff, and run only a few trams along the main road.
Jonah listened to the end and then said politely that a plan which left out the people was not a plan for a city. Mr Garrity smiled as if Jonah had told a small joke.
Mrs Faro said that on Saturday the Board would watch a real test on the city streets. Ines's plan would run on one stretch of the line and Jonah's plan on another.
They prepared for Saturday's test in separate corners of the room. Every time one of them looked up, the other quickly looked down, and the whole office felt the tension.
On Saturday morning the sky was clear and cold, and the Board members stood in a row at Lantern Square. Each of them carried a notebook, and Mr Hale, the chairman, looked at his watch.
Ines's test began first, and the fast trams glided along her stretch of the line. They stopped only twice, and each arrived exactly on time.
Ines felt proud as she watched the Board nod. At the middle stop a small crowd was gathering, and a woman with a pram stood at the very back.
The tram arrived exactly on time and left exactly on time. A woman with a pram ran along the platform toward it, but the doors had already closed, and she stopped, out of breath.
Ines saw the woman standing on the empty platform with her baby, and her stomach dropped. Several members of the Board were writing in their notebooks.
Mrs Adeyemi, the Board member who was a night nurse, spoke quietly to Ines. She said that she often ran for trams after a long shift, and that she had missed a good many.
Then Jonah's test began on a different stretch of the line. His trams stopped often, and at one stop the driver waited while a boy with a heavy school bag ran up and climbed on.
But Jonah's trams quickly became crowded, and all the small stops added up. After half an hour the trams were falling behind the timetable by almost ten minutes.
A driver spoke on the radio and said that he could not keep to time on a line with so many stops. Mr Garrity smiled quietly, and Jonah's face went pale.
The Board went off to a cafe to drink coffee and talk. Mr Hale said nothing at all, and nobody could tell what he was thinking.
They stood by the empty track and neither of them knew what to say. At last Jonah asked in a small voice if she would like to walk, and Ines nodded.
They walked until the afternoon turned to dusk, and then they sat on the Harbour Wall. The water was quiet, and the gulls were settling for the night.
Ines spoke first and said plainly that her fast plan had left a woman with a baby behind. In all her weeks of work she had never once thought about that woman.
Then Jonah told her, just as honestly, that his plan made the whole line crawl. He said that a city cannot run on kindness alone, and that he had been too proud of his idea to see it.
Neither of them wanted to say that the other had been right. In the end they said that they had both been wrong, and then they laughed until they had to wipe their eyes.
They both agreed that the woman with the pram had taught them more than the whole morning. She was running, Jonah said, and they had both seen her, and they could not unsee her.

Ines pulled a paper napkin from her pocket and drew a long straight line on it. Then she added small branches coming off it, like a tree, and said that this could be a fast spine with gentle branches.
Jonah stared at the napkin for a long time without speaking. Then he said, almost in a whisper, that it was the answer, and he began, very quietly, to hum again.
Each of them tried to give the idea to the other, and neither would take it. At last they agreed that it did not belong to either of them, because it belonged to the whole city.

They decided to build one plan together, even though they both knew that only one person could have the job. They bought a bag of hot chips from a stall and ran back to the office, laughing in the cold.
That evening they pushed their desks together and switched on both lamps. Norman the fern sat between them, and the office was quiet except for the sound of pencils.
First they drew the spine along Harbour Road, the long main street of the city. It had only five big stops, far apart, so that the trams could really fly.
Next Jonah drew the branches, small gentle loops that ran into Lantern Square, Cable Lane and Quay Hill. At every branch stop a tram would wait for one minute, just as he had always wanted.
They divided the work between them in a natural way. Ines took the timings and the costs, and Jonah took the stops and the people who would use them.
At last Ines solved the problem of Quay Hill. The depot had two new, light trams with strong brakes, and they could climb the hill on a short branch.
At three in the morning Jonah made a pot of tea and poured it into his blue mug. After a short pause he held the mug out to Ines instead of drinking it himself.
Just before dawn they typed the whole joint timetable into the old Clock, and, for once, it worked. They saved it in five different places, and they did not trust the machine at all.
At sunrise they fell asleep in their chairs with their heads against the window. An hour later they woke up, laughing at their stiff necks, and walked home through the empty streets.
On Monday morning Mrs Faro found the new map pinned on the wall, with two names at the top. She read it all the way through in silence, and then she smiled slowly.
Mrs Faro reminded them that the Board met on Friday and that there was still only one post. But she did not tell them to stop, and she left the map where it was.
On Thursday evening Ines came back to the office to fetch her notebook. Jonah stood by the window with his back to her, talking on his phone in a very low voice.
In the quiet she could hear him very clearly. He said, Yes, Mr Garrity, I will think about it, and then he listened for a long time.
She slipped away down the stairs before he could see her. What offer could Mr Garrity have made, and why would Jonah think about it?
She lay awake all night with old thoughts coming back. She had always known that people who were too kind were hiding something, and now she thought she had been right.
On Friday, the day of the Board, Jonah arrived with two coffees and a cheerful face. He put one on her desk, and Ines did not say thank you.
She stood up and told him, in front of the whole office, that she had heard his call. Her voice shook, and everyone around them stopped what they were doing to listen.
Jonah stood up and said quickly that he had turned the offer down. But Ines was too angry to listen, and she spoke over him again and again.
Tomas and Priya gaped from their desks, and Mina came to the stairs with a ladle in her hand. Priya tried to say Ines's name, but Ines turned away from her too.
Jonah did not shout back at her, but said very quietly that he had thought they were past all this. Then he picked up his blue mug and walked out of the office.
Ines stood alone at her desk for a moment with everyone staring at her. Then she took her coat and walked down the stairs and out into the cold street.
Ines walked to the quay and sat down on a cold bench alone. The wind blew hard off the water, and the gulls circled over her head and cried.
She told herself that she had been right to be careful, and that trusting people was a mistake. But the thought did not comfort her, and she felt sick.
Slowly she remembered everything that Jonah had done for her. He had fixed the printer, circled her mistake, saved the fern and given her his own blue mug at three in the morning.
Then an old man sat down next to her on the bench. He wore a blue cap, and she knew that cheerful, creased face at once because it was Alfie.
Alfie said that Jonah had come to see him that morning and told him everything. He said that Jonah had turned down Mr Garrity's offer, and Ines had not waited to hear it.
Mr Garrity had offered Jonah a high post at his own firm, with a very big salary. All Jonah had to do was withdraw from the contest and let the cheap plan go ahead.
Jonah had said no, Alfie told her, because he would not take a job that left someone behind. He had also said, with a red face, that there was a person he did not want to leave.
Ines whispered that she had not even let Jonah finish. Alfie patted her hand and said that a tram waits for a minute for anyone running, but not all day.
She thanked Alfie with a hug that nearly knocked off his cap. Then she jumped up from the bench and ran back along the quay as fast as she could go.
Back in the office Ines found desk four empty and the blue mug gone. On her own desk lay the finished plan, printed neatly, with both their names on the front.
The note was from Jonah, and it said that he had gone to the Harbour Hall to present the plan alone. It said that her name was first, and that she did not have to come.
Ines grabbed the bound plan and her coat and ran. Priya called out good luck behind her, and Tomas clapped, and Mina shouted something about soup.
Outside, it had begun to rain, hard and cold. The tram to the Harbour Hall was already pulling away from the stop, and Ines was still half a street behind.
The driver saw her in his mirror, a woman running through the rain with a plan in her arms. He stopped the tram and held the doors open, just as Alfie used to do.
The driver smiled and said that Alfie had telephoned him that morning. Alfie had said that someone might be running for the tram today, and that he was to wait for her.
The tram rolled through the rain, stop after stop, and Ines checked her watch again and again. She counted the stops silently, as she had done as a child at the laundry window.
The tram reached the Harbour Hall at last, and Ines jumped down before it had quite stopped. She ran up the wide stone steps with the rain in her eyes and the plan held tight.
At the door a young guard tried to stop her, but she gave her name and said that she was the other planner. He looked at her wet hair, smiled and opened the tall door.
Inside the hall Jonah stood alone before the long table of the Board. An empty chair waited beside him, and Mr Garrity's plan was already glowing on the big screen.
The door opened, and Ines walked into the hall, wet and breathless, and sat down in the empty chair beside him. Jonah turned his head, and his whole face lit up like a lamp.
Ines and Jonah stood up together and presented the plan side by side. Ines explained the timings and the costs, and Jonah described the people who would ride.
Mr Garrity stood up and said that the joint plan was too soft and too costly. Ines answered every one of his numbers calmly, and she showed that it was cheaper in the long run.
Mrs Adeyemi asked what the waiting minute really meant for a tired night nurse. Jonah explained that on the branches a tram would wait one minute for anyone who was running.
While the Board talked in private, Ines and Jonah waited on a bench in the corridor. Ines said she was sorry, and Jonah answered that the tram had still been running.
At last the Board came back, and Mr Hale stood up to speak. He said that they preferred the joint plan of Ines and Jonah to the plan of the consultants, and the hall began to clap.
Mrs Faro stood up with two letters and a very wide smile and said that the Board had made two posts. Ines and Jonah would both be Head of Planning, and they laughed and hugged in front of everyone.
Some weeks later the first test tram of Line 12 ran, and Alfie was asked to drive it. At one stop he waited for a woman with a baby, and Ines and Jonah kissed while he rang the bell.
The next morning Ines bought a bright yellow mug at the depot shop. Jonah said that it would look wonderful next to a blue mug with a chip in it.
Six months later the first public Line 12 tram rolled out exactly on time. At the first branch stop it waited for a girl who was running with her school bag.
Back at the office, desks three and four now stood together as one island under the big window. Jonah's blue mug stood beside Ines's yellow one, and she smiled every time she saw them.

When one was late, she felt it in her shoulders, as though the whole city had missed a step.

Priya was the only person in the office who could tease Ines without being frozen out for a week. Then she leaned over the partition and announced, in a whisper meant to be heard by half the floor, that something was happening.

Tomas, who knew every secret in the building before its owner did, rolled his chair across the floor to share the news. A new planner would start on Monday, he said, and the only empty desk in the room was desk four, directly opposite Ines. He watched her face for a reaction and looked slightly disappointed when she merely blinked.

In the canteen on the ground floor, Mina ladled out her famous leek soup with the solemnity of a priest at a ceremony. Around the long table, the planners traded theories about the newcomer: he was a genius from the capital, said one, or somebody's nephew, said another. Ines ate in silence, quietly sure that nobody wonderful would choose to come to a tram company in a harbour town.

The Clock, as everyone called the company's ancient timetable program, was slow, temperamental and quite capable of swallowing an afternoon's work without warning. Ines had learned its moods the way a sailor learns the weather, saving constantly and trusting nothing. Each timetable that survived it felt to her like a small act of defiance against the machine.

Before leaving for the day, Mrs Faro, the director of planning, paused beside desk three and spoke in the low, level voice she kept for things that mattered. The new planner was very capable, she said, and she hoped that Ines would help him settle in. It was a request, but it was also a quiet warning, and Ines, who was no fool, heard both.

For almost a year Ines had quietly annexed desk four, spreading her maps and route sketches across it as if the territory had always been hers. On Friday afternoon she gathered every sheet into a pile and wiped the bare surface clean, feeling oddly like a person packing up a small and private kingdom. Once it was empty, the desk looked enormous and strangely accusing, as if it already disliked her.

On Sunday evening, as she did every week, Ines telephoned her mother Carmen, who still lived in the narrow street where Ines had been a child. Carmen listened to the whole story of the empty desk and the unknown man, then said that a kind word costs nothing and sometimes buys a great deal. Ines promised to try, in the voice of someone who suspected that she would not.

On Monday morning the director, Mrs Faro, appeared in the doorway with a tall, easy-looking stranger at her side and led him to the empty desk that faced Ines's own. His name was Jonah Pike, and he had come from a small town called Wren Bay to join the planners. Ines gave him a polite nod, but something inside her had already tightened like a drawn curtain.

Jonah leaned across the narrow gap between their desks and offered his hand with a smile so open that it seemed almost unfair. Ines shook it as briefly as courtesy allowed, then informed him, in a tone she hoped was neutral, that the window and its view belonged to desk three. He only nodded, as though she had given him a useful piece of information.

Jonah unpacked his belongings with the unhurried air of a man arriving at a holiday cottage, and the last object out of the box was a blue mug with a chip in its rim. He filled it from the office kettle and began to hum a low, wandering tune that seemed to have no beginning or end. Ines, who valued silence the way other people value money, felt her concentration crumble.

For an hour Ines tried to work through the humming, then quietly stood her pencil case and a stack of folders on the edge of her desk to form a small defensive wall. Jonah noticed it immediately, looked at the barricade with real interest and said nothing at all, which was somehow worse than a joke. She turned back to her screen with her cheeks warm and her mind blank.

That afternoon Jonah asked her, politely, how one persuaded the Clock to save a timetable without losing half of it.
