It was covered with small pencil marks gathered in bundles of five, and she realised with a jolt that he had spent part of the day counting the trams below, exactly as she did. She turned off her lamp quickly, unsettled to find that her rival shared her oldest habit.

On Tuesday morning Mrs Faro rang the little brass bell that she used only for emergencies and good news, and the whole floor gathered in front of her. She held a thin grey folder against her chest, and she waited, with the patience of a woman who has run meetings for twenty years, until the room was perfectly silent. Even Tomas, who whispered through every meeting, had stopped talking and was watching her closely.

The announcement was simple, and it fell on the room like a stone into a pond: the old Line 9, which had carried the city's workers since before most of them were born, would close for good in eight weeks. Its place would be taken by a bold new tramline called Line 12, running from Quay Hill all the way to the Old Docks. Somebody near the back made a small sound like a sigh, and nobody turned to see who it was.

A line of that size, Mrs Faro continued, would need a Head of Planning to guide it, and the company would create precisely one such post. Every person in the room understood immediately that this was the finest job the Harbourgate Tram Company had offered in a generation. Ines felt her heartbeat in her ears, loud and steady, like a clock counting her years.

Mrs Faro explained the method with the calm precision of a surgeon: two planners would each write a complete plan for the new line, and the Board of the city would choose between them. Then she looked first at desk three and next at desk four and said both of their names aloud. Ines turned her head, very slowly, and found Jonah already looking back at her.

The contest, Mrs Faro told them, would run for exactly eight weeks and would end on a Friday afternoon, when the Board gathered at the Harbour Hall to hear both plans and make its choice. Until that day, the two planners would have the same time, the same tools and the same rules, and she herself would give advice but cast no vote. Tomas let out a long, low whistle, as if somebody had just placed an impossible bet on the result.

Jonah turned in his chair, met Ines's eyes and said, with no trace of mockery, that he hoped the best plan would win. She had spent years believing that every contest was a war, and it unsettled her to hear a man speak of one like a friendly game of cards. She nodded stiffly, and the pencil she was holding snapped quietly in her fist.

When the others had returned to their desks, Ines went straight into Mrs Faro's office and asked, without softening it, why a man who had arrived the day before should be allowed to compete for her future. Mrs Faro replied that the Board had asked specifically for fresh eyes, and that Jonah had come with excellent references and a reputation for listening. She added, gently, that nobody had ever won anything by being the only one in the race.

On the Harbour Wall that lunchtime, Ines announced in a flat, fierce voice that she would win the job, and that nothing on earth would stop her. Priya, who had seen her friend skip lunches, holidays and entire weekends, replied quietly that Ines already worked too hard and asked when she planned to rest. Ines said she would rest when the new line opened, and neither of them quite believed it.

That evening Ines opened a fresh notebook and drew a single, confident line from Quay Hill to the Old Docks, with only a handful of stops along it. Her idea was elegant and uncompromising: fast trams, few halts, a journey across the whole city in twenty minutes, a timetable so reliable that people could set their watches by it. She underlined the word speed twice and felt, for the first time that day, entirely like herself.

Across the gap, Jonah worked on a map that could hardly have been more different from hers, crowded with small stops and little handwritten notes beside every one. Reading upside down, which was a skill every planner acquires, Ines could just make out two words repeated along the margin: the waiting minute. She had no idea what they meant, but she disliked them at once, the way one dislikes an unfamiliar dog.

The old printer in the Print Room had been jamming for weeks, and it chose the most inconvenient moment imaginable to do so again. Ines needed her first pages for Mrs Faro by ten o'clock, and the machine merely groaned and swallowed the paper like a stubborn animal refusing its dinner. She had fought it, begged it and finally kicked it, and none of these methods had worked.

She pulled out the crumpled sheets with great care, closed the cover and pressed the button, and the machine jammed for the third time in succession. Ines stood there with her hands on her hips, aware of the minutes disappearing and of a small, hot feeling of defeat gathering behind her eyes. It was only a printer, and she was a grown woman, and yet it was close to making her cry.

Jonah appeared in the doorway of the Print Room holding a small screwdriver and wearing the expression of a doctor who has been called to an emergency. He asked politely whether he might try, and before Ines had arranged a sufficiently cold reply he was already kneeling beside the machine and humming to it. She folded her arms and prepared, with some satisfaction, to watch him fail like everyone before him.

Within ten minutes he had opened three panels, found the cause and held it up between two fingers: a stub of pencil, jammed deep in one of the rollers, probably dropped years ago by some forgotten clerk. Jonah grinned at it as though it were a rare and charming beetle, while Ines stared at the small yellow stub with a mixture of relief and rage. She had been defeated for weeks by something that was no bigger than her thumb, and she could not decide whether to laugh.

When the machine had finally begun to purr, Jonah stepped aside, let Ines's pages roll out before his own and presented them to her with a small, gallant bow. She thanked him in a voice as cold as the harbour in January, and it seemed to her that his smile only grew warmer, which was entirely unfair. A rival who rescued you, she thought, was far harder to dislike than one who simply obstructed you.

By lunchtime Tomas had spread the story through every desk and corridor of the building, with improvements, until the pencil stub had become a small iron bolt and the ten minutes had shrunk to five. Several colleagues clapped Jonah on the back as he passed, and one even offered him a biscuit, while Ines bent over her figures and pretended not to notice. Priya, who was watching her across the room, hid a wide smile behind a paper cup of lukewarm coffee.

On the stairs that afternoon Priya told Ines, with the gentle firmness of an old friend, that Jonah was a gift to the whole office and might even be a gift to Ines herself. Ines retorted that he was not a gift but a threat, and that kind people were the most dangerous rivals because everyone wanted them to win. Priya shook her head and said that was the saddest argument she had ever heard.

All that week Ines worked until nine o'clock every evening, bent over her screen in the pool of her lamp, while Jonah put on his coat at five and strolled off to walk beside the harbour. When she remarked on it, with an edge she did not trouble to hide, he answered cheerfully that tired minds make bad timetables, and that the best ideas came to him on the water. She wrote that down in her head as the excuse of a man who was not working hard enough.

On Thursday night she ate a box of cold noodles at her desk, looking out at the harbour where the ferry lights drifted like small, slow stars. The office was so quiet that she could hear the wall clock ticking, and the familiar silence, which she had always loved, felt for the first time like an empty room rather than a calm one. She could not have said exactly when the difference had begun, only that it had arrived quietly and stayed.

On Friday morning Jonah arrived with two warm pastries from the bakery on Cable Lane and set one gently on the corner of Ines's desk. She declined it with exaggerated politeness, pushing the paper bag back across the gap, and Tomas, who had been hovering nearby with the hunger of a seagull, claimed it before it touched the table. Jonah only laughed at the pastry thief, and the warm sound of it followed her all through the long morning.

In the second week Mrs Faro asked both planners to survey the crossing at Gull Street, the busiest junction on the whole proposed line. Neither said a word to the other, and yet each independently decided on Wednesday at dawn, when the first workers of the day pour toward the harbour. Ines discovered the coincidence only when she arrived at the crossing and found him already standing there.

Ines reached Gull Street at six o'clock with a stopwatch, a clipboard and a fixed intention of being first. Jonah was already there, leaning against a lamp post with a flask of steaming tea and an expression of perfect contentment, and he waved to her as though he had been waiting for a friend. She could have sworn that the sky was still grey when she had left her flat.

Both of them stepped forward to begin counting at precisely the same instant, and their clipboards collided with a clack that sent a dozen sheets fluttering into the road. For a full minute two respectable planners chased paper between the early cars, bending and dodging and muttering apologies, while a bus driver leaned on his horn and grinned. When it was over, they stood panting on the kerb, and Jonah was laughing.

For an hour they stood on opposite corners of the junction and counted every rider who stepped off a tram, using methods that proved to be completely different. When they compared their sheets, the totals were far apart, and both of them stiffened, each privately certain that the error was the other's. It was a petty disagreement about a few dozen people, but it felt, to Ines, like a matter of principle.

While Ines concentrated on her tally, Jonah drifted among the people waiting at the stop, asking each of them politely why they always seemed to be in such a hurry. Ines informed him, when he returned with a handful of scribbled notes, that numbers were facts and stories were merely stories, and that a plan could only be built on the former. Jonah answered that numbers told you where people were, but not why they ran.

Back in the office they spread a vast map across the meeting table and began, politely at first, to demolish each other's ideas. Ines wanted fast trams with very few stops, so that the city could cross itself in twenty minutes, while Jonah wanted frequent stops and trams that would wait, just briefly, for the people who were running. Neither of them noticed that the others in the room had stopped working to listen.

As the argument gathered speed their voices rose together, each interrupting the other with another fact, another objection, another map pin stabbed into the paper. Tomas slid slowly down behind his computer screen, as if sheltering from a storm, and Priya raised a single eyebrow so high that it almost reached her hairline. The only person who seemed to be enjoying himself was Jonah, which made Ines angrier still.

Mrs Faro walked in at the height of the quarrel, held up one hand for silence and listened, without interrupting, to both ideas from beginning to end. She praised each of them with exactly the same warmth, and when Ines pressed her to name a favourite, she only smiled and remarked that the question belonged to the Board. She left the room as calmly as she had entered it, and everybody inside began again, slowly, to breathe.

Afterwards Ines was furious with herself for having raised her voice in front of the whole office, which she had not done in six years of service. On the stairs Jonah caught up with her and said, with every sign of sincerity, that the argument had been the best part of his week, because nobody had ever pushed back so hard. She stared at him, completely speechless, while he went on down the steps with that wandering tune of his.

On the tram home that evening Ines found herself remembering one of the scribbled notes Jonah had waved at her, the one she had pretended to ignore. A woman at the stop had said that she did not need a fast tram at all, only a tram that was still there when she finally arrived at the platform. It was a small sentence, but it sat in Ines's mind for the rest of the night like a pebble in a shoe.

One night in the third week, Ines was working alone in the dark office when she noticed Jonah's folder sitting on the shared server, unlocked and unguarded. She told herself she would only look at the title, and then, with the small thrill of a person breaking a rule, she opened the plan and began to read. It was not an act she was proud of, and she did it anyway.

His plan was clear, humane and astonishingly thorough: every stop carried notes about the real people who would use it, from school children to night nurses. At each one he had proposed what he called the waiting minute, a brief pause that would let a running passenger reach the doors, and the more she read, the more sensible it sounded. She closed the file at last with a sinking feeling that his plan was genuinely good.

She sat very still for a while, uncomfortable at having read what was not hers to read and more uncomfortable still at what she had found. Beneath the guilt lay a colder and more shameful feeling, a fear that the man across the desk might actually be better at this work than she was. She had never before had to consider that possibility, and it was oddly like standing at the edge of a cliff.

The following morning a yellow note was waiting on Ines's map, and beside it a small pencil circle drew her eye to a minute error in the curve at Lantern Square. She checked it twice, and then a third time, and each time she was obliged to admit that Jonah was perfectly right. A tram of that length could never have made the turn, and her whole beautiful speed would have collapsed there.

Determined not to be outdone, Ines spent the entire afternoon combing through Jonah's published figures until she found a single misplaced decimal buried deep in a table of passenger counts. She circled it in red pencil with a small flourish and left the page on his chair, feeling grimly pleased with herself. At last, she thought with quiet satisfaction, the account between the two of them had been settled.

Jonah read the red circle on his page, looked up across the desks and thanked her with such real warmth that it seemed he had received a present. Ines had prepared herself for a quarrel, or at least a scowl, and being thanked instead felt like being tickled by a feather in the middle of a battle. She spent the rest of the afternoon wondering what kind of man treated his own mistakes as gifts.

That week an undeclared and entirely childish war began, and Ines fired the opening shot by lowering Jonah's chair as far as the mechanism would permit. When he sat down his chin ended up almost level with the desktop, and the whole office pretended not to look while he, to her great irritation, simply threw back his head and laughed. She had planned a victory, and she had somehow supplied him with a joke.

On the following morning Ines found that her fern, Norman, had been moved to a sunnier corner of the windowsill and propped on a small folded cloth. By the afternoon the poor plant looked greener and more cheerful than it had in a year, and Ines, who had come prepared to be furious, discovered that she had nothing to be furious about. It was an act of kindness, and kindness was the one weapon she had no answer to.

In a moment of weakness Ines hid Jonah's chipped blue mug at the back of a cupboard, and when tea time came he cheerfully brewed his drink in a jam jar borrowed from the canteen. He seemed perfectly content, holding the hot glass with a folded napkin and humming as always, and she felt so ashamed that she returned the mug before lunch. He looked at it, looked at her and said nothing, and that was the kindest silence she had ever received.

At the end of the third week Priya leaned across the partition and observed that Ines, for the first time in years, looked as though she were enjoying her work. Ines called the idea nonsense, and she called it so firmly that Priya only nodded and returned to her desk with an infuriating look of private triumph. The truth, which neither of them mentioned, was that Ines had been smiling when Priya arrived.

In the fourth week a stubborn Monday rain set in, and by nine o'clock the water had risen over the rails at the junction of Gull Street. The trams stopped one behind another in a long, glistening line, and soon the whole city seemed to be running late, like a clock that had been dropped. In the planners' room, every one of the telephones began to ring all at the same time.

Mrs Faro put down the telephone, looked at the two rival desks and sent both planners straight out into the weather to repair the schedule on the spot. A plan on paper, she reminded them crisply, was only worth anything if it survived a flood, and she handed each of them a heavy yellow raincoat from the cupboard. Ines noticed that Jonah's was far too short in the arms, and she was ashamed of how much it pleased her.

The tram was crowded, steaming and smelling of wet wool, and Ines found herself pressed so close to Jonah that she could feel him humming through his coat. He had opened his umbrella over an elderly woman who had no hat, and he stood with the rain dripping down his collar, apparently unaware of his own discomfort. Ines looked at the floor, then at the window, and then, against her better judgement, at him.

Without being asked, Jonah told her that his grandfather had driven the old Line 9 for forty years, and he held out his phone to show her a faded photograph of a grinning man in a blue cap. It was the first time that Ines had seen him look at anything with such plain, unguarded love. She understood suddenly that the line she was planning to replace was, to him, a family home.

The old man's name was Alfie, Jonah explained, and he was seventy-eight years old, still very funny and quietly heartbroken that his beloved line was to close. He would never admit to being sad, Jonah added, because he had always told his passengers that a tram driver's job was to be cheerful until the last stop. Ines swallowed, because she had never thought about the people who would lose something when her new line arrived.

To her own astonishment, Ines found herself telling him that she had grown up in a cramped flat above Bright Laundry on Cable Lane, where the windows had steamed up every winter. As a small girl she had counted the passing buses to pass the time, and that was how she had first fallen in love with timetables. Jonah listened without interrupting, and he did not once make a joke, which was exactly what she had needed.

At last the tram slowed and shuddered to a halt at Gull Street, with the water lapping at the lowest step and the anxious passengers murmuring among themselves. A small child began to cry, and the driver announced, with an apologetic shrug, that he could not take the carriage another metre. Ines looked at Jonah, and Jonah looked at Ines, and for once they had precisely the same thought.

Standing in the downpour, they spoke into the depot radio by turns and finished each other's sentences, sending two trams around the flooded crossing by a long loop through Lantern Square. Neither of them could have said afterwards who had first suggested it, and the scheme worked so smoothly that the driver gaped at them as if they had performed a conjuring trick. It was the first plan they had ever made together, and neither of them remarked on it.

Soaked to the skin and shivering, they sheltered beneath the awning of a street kiosk and shared two paper cups of scalding tea, steam rising from their sleeves like smoke. Jonah made a joke about the length of their yellow raincoats, and Ines heard herself laugh out loud, a sound she had not made in front of a colleague for as long as she could remember. He looked quietly delighted, as if he had just won something far more valuable than any contest.

When the two of them finally returned to the office, dripping onto the floor and unusually quiet, Priya looked from one to the other and took in the wet hair and the bright eyes. She asked, with studied innocence, what had happened at Gull Street, and Ines answered rather too quickly that nothing whatsoever had happened. Priya smiled into her coffee, and she did not say another word about it for the rest of that whole day.

On Wednesday afternoon the ancient Clock, which had survived fourteen years of abuse, let out one long mournful beep and turned its screen a deep and hopeless blue. A line of strange letters crawled across it, and nothing that Ines pressed, however firmly, made the slightest difference. Across the desks she heard Jonah say a very quiet word that was not in any timetable.

It soon became clear that the crash had swallowed everything the two planners had done since the previous morning, every revised route and every carefully balanced timing. They sat in silence staring at identical blue screens, each privately remembering the backup they had meant to make and had not. The silence in the office was so complete that Norman the fern seemed to be listening.

Tomas, who had been sent to find help, returned with the dismal news that the only person who understood the Clock was on a beach somewhere for another week. There was no copy of their work anywhere in the building, he said, and he looked genuinely sorry, which made the news rather harder to bear. Ines closed her eyes and counted slowly to ten, as her mother had once taught her.

It was Jonah who broke the silence, proposing in a calm voice that they simply rebuild everything by hand, and he fetched a vast roll of plain white paper from the Print Room. Ines opened her mouth to say that it was a foolish and old-fashioned idea, and then she realised that she had nothing better to offer. She took the ruler that he handed her, and she knelt down beside him on the floor.

They knelt side by side on the floorboards with rulers, erasers and a row of sharpened pencils, and they began to redraw the timetables, line by careful line, as planners had done long before computers existed. Slowly the white paper filled with tidy columns of times, and the work became strangely peaceful, almost like a game that two children play when the rain keeps them indoors. For hours and hours, neither of them so much as glanced at the clock on the wall.

At six o'clock Jonah produced a slightly squashed sandwich from his bag and, without any ceremony, cut it neatly in half with a ruler. A little later Mina, who had heard of the disaster from Tomas, sent up two steaming bowls of her best leek soup on a tray, and the pair of them ate cross-legged on the floor among the sheets of paper. Ines could not remember the last time that a simple meal had tasted so good to her.

As the columns filled with numbers, both of them stopped at once and pointed at the same place on the map, their fingers almost touching. Quay Hill, the very steep street that the new line would have to climb, was a problem that neither plan had properly solved, since a slow and heavy tram could scarcely crawl up it in the wet. For a moment they simply stared at each other, each waiting for the other to speak.

Ines saw that her fast trams would be too heavy and hurried for the climb, while Jonah saw that his patient, frequent trams would take an hour to crawl up it. Neither of them said so aloud, because to say so would have meant admitting that the contest was no longer simple, and for the moment they were both content to leave it unspoken. They went back to their pencils without another word, and the silence between them felt new and rather careful.

By midnight the paper timetables were complete, every column checked twice and every number correct, and the floor around them looked like the aftermath of a small and very orderly snowstorm. They sat with their backs against the desks and began to laugh, helplessly, from sheer tiredness and relief, until Ines had to wipe her eyes with her sleeve. It was the happiest she had been in the building in years, and it frightened her.

Mrs Faro arrived early the next morning and paused in the doorway, taking in the sheets of paper, the sleepy faces and the sight of two supposed rivals laughing together over a cold cup of tea. She said nothing for a long moment, and then, in the gentlest voice she owned, she reminded them that only one of them could win the post. Neither of them answered her, and all the laughter drained quietly out of the room like water from a bath.

That night, in her small and perfectly tidy flat, Ines lay awake and stared at the ceiling while the harbour lights slid slowly across it. She had always answered the question of ambition with energy rather than thought, and now, for the first time, she asked herself honestly why she wanted this particular job so badly. The answer did not come at once, and when it did, it came from a long way back.

She remembered her mother Carmen, who for years had cleaned the offices of the city at night, pushing a heavy grey cart from floor to floor while the building slept. When Ines was small and no one could look after her, she had gone along too, and she had sat in the corridors with a book on her knees, listening to the polishing machine hum in the distance. Those silent, shining corridors were the first offices that she had ever known, and she had never forgotten them.

In one of those offices a well-dressed planner had often worked late, and he had never once looked up at the woman who emptied his bin. The little girl under the desk had made herself a promise, in the fierce silent way that children make such promises, that one day she would be the person at the desk. She would also, she had sworn, always say good evening to the cleaner, and both halves of that promise had mattered to her ever since.

On Sunday Ines took the tram out to Cable Lane to visit her mother, as she did whenever she could, and climbed the narrow stairs beside Bright Laundry that she had climbed ten thousand times as a child. Carmen still lived in the very same small flat above the shop, and the kettle was already warm on the stove, as though the old woman had felt her daughter coming. The warm smell of clean sheets and hot irons drifted up the stairwell behind her as she climbed, and it felt like coming home.

Carmen poured the tea, sat down by the window and listened without interrupting to the whole story of the contest, the rival, the plans and the plain exhaustion. When it was over she remarked, in her slow and unhurried way, that a prize won alone is a very lonely thing, and that she had learned it on the night shift. Ines opened her mouth to argue, then closed it again and drank her tea.

Carmen asked, with a gleam in her eye, what kind of man this Jonah was, and Ines replied, very stiffly, that he was her rival and nothing else. Her mother laughed so hard that she had to put down her cup and press a hand to her chest, and when Ines demanded to know what was so funny, she only shook her head. It was the first time in weeks that Ines had seen her mother truly amused.

Before leaving, Ines stood at the old window above the street where she had once spent her whole childhood and, without deciding to, began counting the buses. There were far fewer than in her girlhood, and the street seemed quieter and smaller, and the people waiting at the bus stop looked older and more tired than she remembered. She wondered, for the first time, who was left behind when a city sped up.

On Monday morning Ines glanced across the two desks and noticed that Jonah looked as tired as she felt, with untidy hair, ink on his cuff and dark smudges under his eyes. It dawned on her slowly that he had been working through the weekend too, and that the man who left at five every evening was no more relaxed about the contest than she was. She had been so busy resenting his calm that she had never looked behind it.

Jonah held out an old paper ticket and asked, a little shyly, whether she would ride Line 9 with him at dawn on Thursday, because the line would close the following week. He said he wanted to see it one last time with someone who understood trams, and he added, as an afterthought, that his grandfather would be there too. It was an invitation that was not really about work at all, and it sounded like a small, sincere gift.

Ines told him quite firmly that she had far too much work and could not possibly spare the time, and she said it in the brisk voice she used for refusing meetings. Jonah only nodded and left the paper ticket on the corner of her desk, saying that the offer would stand until the tram actually left. All that evening she tried not to look at the small rectangle of card, and she failed completely.

On Thursday, long before the sun was up, Ines assured herself that she was simply going to the office early to work in peace. Instead her feet carried her, as if of their own will, to the old Line 9 platform at the end of Gull Street, where she stood in the cold with the paper ticket crushed in her pocket. She told herself that she had only come to look at the tram, and she did not believe it.

Jonah was already waiting on the platform in the pale blue light, holding two paper cups of tea that sent up two small plumes of steam. He did not look in the least surprised to see her, and he simply handed her a cup, as though he had never doubted that she would come. Ines took it and said nothing, because anything she said would have been a confession.

Then the old yellow tram of Line 9 slid out of the half dark and glided into the station with its lights still burning, its brass handles gleaming and its wheels humming softly on the rails. Behind it the sky was turning from grey to rose, and the whole street seemed to hold its breath, as if it knew that this was something that would not happen again. It was a beautiful sight, far more beautiful than Ines had expected, and she found that she could not look away.

In the very first seat of the carriage, wrapped in a patched woollen coat and wearing the blue cap from the photograph, sat an old man with a face like a friendly walnut. This was Alfie, Jonah's grandfather, who had come at the very first hour to say goodbye to the line that had been his working life. He stood up with some effort and shook Ines's hand with both of his.

Alfie settled back into his seat and explained, with a perfectly straight face, that he had been late for his own wedding, his own birthday and most of his cousins' funerals. But in forty years of service on Line 9, he said, he had never once been late for work, and the tram had never once been late for him. Ines laughed out loud before she could stop herself, and she saw Jonah smile down at his shoes.

The tram rolled out along the edge of the harbour, rocking gently, while the sun lifted itself over the water and set the cranes and the ships and the long wet quays on fire with gold. Nobody said anything for a while, and the only sound was the old wheels singing on the rails, a note that Ines thought she would remember for the rest of her life. She pressed her forehead against the cool glass of the window, and she let herself simply look at it all.

Alfie raised one finger and told them the single rule that had governed his whole career: he never closed the doors of his tram while somebody was still running toward it. Other drivers had mocked him for the lost seconds, he said, but he had always found that a minute spent waiting was a minute that the city got back many times over. Jonah, listening, nodded as if he had heard it a hundred times and never tired of it.

One winter night, Alfie said, a young woman had come running down the street toward his tram carrying a small suitcase and holding her side. He had waited with the doors open, and had driven her without stopping all the way to the hospital, where she arrived with minutes to spare and her first child was born before morning. Years later, he added with a slow smile, the grown child had come all the way to the depot just to thank him.

Ines listened with a lump rising in her throat, aware that the warm light on the old wooden seats was making everything look painfully dear. When at last she turned her head, she found that Jonah was not looking at the harbour, or at his grandfather, but straight at her, with an expression so gentle that she had to look away. Her heart did something complicated and entirely unprofessional, and for once she did not try to give it orders.

At the last stop, down at the Old Docks, Alfie climbed slowly out and patted the yellow side of the old tram like the neck of a faithful horse. He turned to the two young planners and said, quietly and without any speech, that the city needed whatever came next to remember one thing: that people run, and a good tram waits for them. Then he put on his blue cap, nodded to them both and walked slowly away along the quay into the morning.

Back at the office Ines sat in front of a blank page for an entire hour, unable to write a single useful line. Alfie's quiet words about people who run kept returning to her mind, and with them came the image of the woman at the stop who only wanted the tram to be there. Her beautiful fast line suddenly looked very cold and rather lonely on the paper.

At last Ines stood up, crossed the little gap between their desks and swallowed her pride in a single painful gulp. She asked Jonah, as politely as she had ever asked anything, whether she might use his idea of a waiting minute in her own plan. It was the hardest sentence she had spoken in years, and it left her feeling slightly dizzy.

Jonah looked startled at first, then pleased, and then he told her, with a smile that reached all the way to his eyes, that she should take the idea and welcome. A good idea, he said, only does any good when somebody uses it, and he would rather see it on a real street than in a drawer. It was the most generous thing anyone had said to her in months, and it left her strangely disarmed.

Then, because she could not leave a generous act unanswered, Ines proposed that from this day the contest should be a fair fight, with no more lowered chairs, hidden mugs or secret raids on the server. Jonah agreed immediately and added, with a perfectly serious face, that he had never really enjoyed the chair trick anyway. She smiled in spite of herself, and she found that she could not quite stop.

They shook hands across the narrow gap between the desks to seal the bargain, and the handshake went on a little longer than a handshake had any business to last. Neither of them seemed to notice until the entire office had fallen silent, with Tomas frozen mid-sentence and Priya staring with her coffee halfway to her mouth. Ines let go first, and her hand felt warm for the rest of the morning.

Now the meeting of the Board was only two weeks away, and both planners returned to their long evenings, though the atmosphere in the room had quietly changed. They no longer guarded their screens or hid their notes, and they lent each other numbers and pencils without any pretence of reluctance. The rivalry was still there, but it had begun to look much more like a race between friends.

One night they ate takeaway noodles in the Print Room, perched on the edge of the table among maps and drafts and cold cups of tea. Jonah, to his deep embarrassment, could not hold chopsticks at all, and Ines, laughing, demonstrated with two sharpened pencils until he finally lifted a single noodle into the air. He cheered as loudly as though he had won the Board's approval, and the whole corridor must have heard him.

Late in the week they tested the timings of the proposed line with a stopwatch, one stop and one minute at a time, checking each against the other's numbers. Jonah hummed as he counted, as he always did, and Ines noticed with some alarm that the sound which had once driven her to build a wall of folders had become something she found almost comforting. At one point she caught herself humming along with him, quite badly and entirely out of tune, and he politely pretended not to hear.

At lunch Priya informed her friend, in the casual tone of someone reporting the weather, that Ines had recently begun to hum at her desk. Ines called the claim ridiculous and slanderous, and then, in the middle of her protest, became aware that she was humming the very tune that Jonah played all day long. Priya raised both hands in the air, as if the case were closed and the judge had gone home for the evening.

That afternoon Ines realised, with a faint sense of alarm, that she looked up every single time the door of the office opened, and that she was always hoping for the same tall figure. She told herself that it meant nothing, that it was only habit, that any planner would watch the door of a busy room, and none of these explanations was convincing. She bent over her work with great determination, and her face felt very warm for the rest of the afternoon.

On Friday afternoon the radio announced a severe storm warning, and the sky above the harbour grew darker with every passing minute. The sea turned the colour of old iron, the gulls vanished from the quay, and the first great drops of rain began to slap against the office windows like thrown coins. Everybody in the building began to gather their coats and umbrellas and hurry toward the stairs in an anxious little crowd.

One by one the colleagues drifted out, wishing each other a safe journey, until only the two rival planners remained in the great echoing room with their lamps lit. Each had told themselves that a few more hours would finish the draft, and each had privately decided not to be the first to leave. Mrs Faro, passing on her way out, told them sternly to go home soon.

At about eight o'clock a great fork of lightning split the sky and lit up the whole harbour in a single white instant, and the thunder arrived almost on top of it. The windows rattled in their frames, the lamps on the desks flickered like candles in a draught, and Ines gripped the edge of her desk with both hands. Jonah, across from her, had stopped humming for the first time all day, and she noticed the sudden absence of it.

Then every light in the office died at the same moment, and the hum of the computers sank away to nothing, leaving a darkness so complete that Ines could not see her own hands. Outside the window the street lamps, the crane lights and the lit-up windows of the harbour had all vanished, as though somebody had folded the city up and put it away. The silence that followed was enormous, and it seemed to press against the windows from both the inside and the outside.

They carried their phones to the floor by the big window and sat down with their backs against the wall, side by side, the two small lights making a pair of pale circles on the carpet. The rain drummed steadily against the glass, and the dark harbour lay beyond it like the inside of a great, sleeping animal. After a minute, Jonah said that it was rather beautiful, and Ines found that she agreed.

In the dark, honesty seemed to come more easily than it ever did in daylight, and Jonah admitted quietly that he was afraid of losing the contest. He did not mind for himself, he explained, but his grandfather had always told the neighbours that his grandson would run the new line, and Jonah could not bear the thought of letting the old man down. His voice was small and rather rough, and Ines did not interrupt him, because she understood that he was trusting her.

Then, because he had been brave, Ines found herself being brave too, and she confessed that her own deepest fear was of being ordinary. All her life she had worked and counted and planned so that she would never be nobody, and she lay awake at night afraid that all that effort would end in nothing at all. Saying it out loud felt like setting down a very heavy bag that she had been carrying for most of her life.

Jonah turned his head and said, in a voice that left no room for argument, that she was the least ordinary person he had ever met in his life. Ines laughed, but it was a shaky and uncertain laugh, and she noticed in the dim light that their hands were lying side by side on the carpet, with only a finger's breadth between them. Neither of them moved at all, and somewhere far out over the sea the storm went rolling slowly away into the night.

Slowly, as if each of them were afraid of startling the other, they leaned toward one another in the dark until their faces were only a few centimetres apart. Ines could hear her own heart thumping in her ears like a tram on a long bridge, and she was almost certain that Jonah could hear it as well. For one long, suspended moment, nothing at all in the world seemed more important than what was about to happen.

At that precise moment every light in the room flickered and blazed back to life, the computers woke with a chorus of beeps, and the harbour glittered through the glass as though nothing had ever happened. The two of them sprang apart like children caught stealing biscuits, and both began at once to speak, very quickly and in loud voices, about the Clock and the probable state of the files. In the confusion Jonah knocked over his blue mug, and it rolled across the desk and, to everyone's relief, did not break.

On Monday morning Ines arrived at the office earlier than anyone, arranged her pencils into an unusually rigid line and kept her eyes fixed on her screen as though it contained a matter of life and death. When Jonah came in and wished her a warm good morning, she answered him with a single stiff nod and did not look up. All weekend she had rehearsed what she might say, and in the event she said nothing.

Jonah seemed to understand without being told, and with a courtesy she found almost unbearable he gathered his laptop, his notes and his blue mug and walked to a table at the far end. His chair at desk four stood empty, and the gap between the desks suddenly looked as wide as the harbour. She told herself that this was exactly what she had wanted, and the thought was not much comfort.

Priya noticed within an hour that the two planners had stopped speaking to each other altogether, and that the old teasing had been replaced by a careful, courteous silence. Even Tomas, who adored any kind of office drama, remarked that the quiet felt wrong, as if a bright clock had stopped in the middle of the room. Priya made a firm note in her head to speak to her friend alone at lunch, whether or not Ines wished it.

At lunch on the Harbour Wall Priya asked directly what had happened on the night of the storm, and Ines replied, much too quickly, that nothing whatsoever had happened. Priya looked at her for a long moment, then said very gently that Ines did not have to be honest with her, but she did have to be honest with herself. Ines stared at the grey waves for a very long time without answering, because she knew that her friend was right.

Mrs Faro called both of them into her office that afternoon and closed the door, which she rarely did, and told them that the Board was becoming nervous about the cost of the whole project. A firm of outside consultants had made an offer of their own, a cheap and simple plan, and several members of the Board were beginning to like the price. Unless both plans impressed them, she said, the job might never go to either of them.

The next day Mr Garrity himself arrived to inspect the office, a tall man in a smooth grey suit who smiled at everybody and looked at the furniture as though he were wondering what it might fetch. He shook every hand in the room with the same bright, practised warmth and gave each person a business card on thick cream paper. Ines disliked him with a speed and a strength that surprised her, and she suspected that Jonah would soon feel just the same.

Mr Garrity showed the planners his plan on a gleaming screen, with the confidence of a man who sells such things every week. He proposed to cut the number of stops by half, reduce the staff and run a small number of trams along the main road only, and he called the result efficient and modern. He added that Jonah's idea was sentimental, and Ines's, though tidy, was an expensive dream.

Jonah listened to the whole presentation without interrupting, and when it was over he said, in his mildest voice, that a plan without the people who run was not a plan for a city. Mr Garrity smiled and nodded with the air of a man who is kindly humouring a clever child. Ines felt a surge of anger on Jonah's behalf that took her entirely by surprise.

Mrs Faro explained the arrangements for the Board's inspection with her usual calm precision: on Saturday morning, before the Board's own eyes, each plan would be tested on the real rails of the real city. Ines's plan would run along one stretch of the route and Jonah's along another, and both would be judged by what actually happened to the riders. Neither planner said a single word, because both of them knew very well how cruel a real test can be.

All week they prepared for the Saturday test in separate corners of the room, and they exchanged only the stiff, necessary messages of colleagues who have a task in common. Each time one of them looked up and caught the other's eye, both of them looked quickly away, and the whole floor held its breath and pretended not to notice. On Friday evening Ines took out her phone, wrote Jonah a message and then deleted every word of it.

On Saturday morning the sky was washed clean and the light was cold and bright, and the members of the Board stood in a solemn row at Lantern Square with their notebooks open. Mr Hale, the grey-haired chairman, checked his pocket watch with the air of a man who had seen many plans fail, while Mrs Adeyemi, a night nurse who sat on the Board, stamped her feet against the chill. Mr Garrity hovered at the edge of the group, smiling gently at nothing in particular as he waited for the show to begin.

Ines's test came first, and for a while it went better than even she had dared to imagine. The fast trams glided down her stretch of the line like beads on a string, stopping only twice, and each one arrived at the second that her timetable had promised. The Board members glanced at their watches and nodded, and one of them murmured something that sounded very much like admiration.

Ines felt her chest swell with a pride that she did not trouble to hide, for the speed of the trams and the nods of the Board were exactly what she had worked for during all those late nights. At the middle stop a modest crowd was gathering for the next carriage, and at the very back of it stood a young woman with a pram and a heavy bag. She was walking quickly, but she was at the wrong end of the platform.

The tram arrived with perfect punctuality, and with equal punctuality its doors began to close, exactly as the timetable demanded. The young woman with the pram broke into a run along the platform, one hand on the handle and the other waving, but the carriage was already moving, and she stopped, breathless, and watched its lights shrink down the line. The driver had done absolutely nothing wrong, and that was precisely the problem, as Ines was beginning to understand.

Ines saw the young woman standing alone on the empty platform, jiggling her pram gently and looking at the place where the tram had been, and something cold dropped through her stomach. All along the row the Board members bent over their notebooks and began to write, and she knew with miserable certainty exactly what they were writing. The beautiful, punctual line had a gap in it the shape of one person.

Mrs Adeyemi, the Board member who worked nights as a nurse at the harbour hospital, came and stood beside Ines and spoke in a low voice that carried no blame at all. She said that she ran for trams most mornings after a long shift and had missed a good many of them over the years. Each missed tram, she added, had felt a little like being told that she did not count.

Then it was Jonah's turn, on a different stretch of the route, and the character of the morning changed completely. His trams stopped often and politely, and at one small stop the driver held the doors for a full minute while a boy with a heavy school bag came pounding up the street and clambered aboard, gasping his thanks. Mrs Adeyemi wrote something in her notebook with great care, and then she underlined the words twice and nodded slowly.

As the morning went on, however, the picture became less cheerful, for the frequent stops multiplied and the carriages filled until the people inside stood pressed together like sardines in a tin. Every kindly minute of waiting added itself to the next, and after half an hour Jonah's trams had fallen almost ten minutes behind the timetable, and the line was beginning to crawl. A baby began to cry somewhere near the back, and a tired man gave up his seat to an old lady.

A driver's voice crackled from the radio, tired and not at all gentle, complaining that no one could possibly keep to a timetable on a line with so many stops. Mr Garrity, standing at the edge of the group, allowed himself a quiet and satisfied smile, and Jonah, who had been watching his trams with such hope, went pale to the lips. Ines saw it all and felt the pain of it as though it were her own.

At last the Board retired to a nearby cafe to drink coffee and compare their notes in private, and the little group of observers drifted apart across the square. Mr Hale, who had said not one word throughout the whole morning, walked off in the middle of them with his hands behind his back, and not even Mrs Faro could guess what he was thinking. The test was finally over, and yet in spite of everything that had happened nothing at all had been decided.

For a long time the two of them stood side by side beside the empty rails, in a silence made heavier by everything that neither of them could think how to say. At last Jonah asked, in a small and uncertain voice, whether she would like to walk, and Ines, who had spent the week avoiding him, found herself nodding at once. They set off together toward the harbour, with no particular plan except to keep walking in the cold clean air.

They walked for the rest of the afternoon without caring where they went, and when the sky began to turn pink and gold they found themselves sitting on the Harbour Wall, with their legs hanging over the water. The harbour was quiet, the gulls were settling on the cranes for the night, and somewhere far off a ship's horn gave a long, low note. It was the same wall where Ines ate lunch each day, and tonight it felt entirely different.

Ines spoke first, and for once she did not dress it up in numbers or defend herself against anyone. Her fast plan, she said plainly, had left a woman and her baby standing alone on a platform, and in six weeks of careful calculating she had never once thought about that woman at all. It was a shameful thing to admit, and it was also a huge relief.

Then Jonah answered with the same honesty, and he did not spare himself either. His gentle plan, he admitted, had made the whole line crawl, with every kind little minute stacking up against the next, and a city could not be run on kindness alone however much he might wish it. He confessed that he had been so pleased with his idea that he had refused to look at its faults.

Neither of them could quite bring themselves to say the words you were right, for each had spent far too long believing the opposite, and the silence that followed was almost comical. In the end it was Ines who said that they had probably both been wrong, and Jonah who said that it was a great comfort, and then they laughed until they had to lean against each other on the stones. The sound of their laughter rang out over the quiet harbour, and even a sleepy gull lifted its head to look at them.

They both agreed, after a thoughtful pause, that the young woman with the pram had taught them more than all the rest of the long morning put together. She had been running, Jonah said, and he and Ines had both seen her, and having seen her they could never again design a line that forgot her. Neither of them mentioned the Board or the prize, and for a little while that felt like the truth.

Ines pulled a crumpled napkin from her coat pocket, took out a pencil and drew a single long straight line across it, fast and bold. Then, almost without thinking, she added small curving branches coming off it at intervals, until the drawing looked like a young tree, and she said, slowly, that this might be a fast spine with gentle branches. The trams on the spine could rush, she explained, while the branches could wait for people.

Jonah took the napkin in both hands and stared at it for so long that Ines began to wonder if she had made some terrible mistake. Then he looked up, with his whole face alight, and said in an almost reverent whisper that it was the answer, that it had always been the answer, and that they had needed each other to find it. Very softly, as if he were talking only to himself, he began to hum the old wandering tune that she had once hated.

A friendly argument followed in which each of them tried vigorously to give the credit to the other, Ines insisting that the branches were pure Jonah and Jonah insisting that the spine was pure Ines. At last they agreed, in the manner of people who have found something larger than themselves, that the idea belonged to neither of them but to the city, and that all they had done was to notice it. They shook hands again, as solemnly as two diplomats, and neither of them let go of the other's hand too quickly.

Then, with a clarity that surprised them both, they decided to build one plan together, knowing perfectly well that this might cost one or both of them the post for which they had worked so hard. They bought a paper bag of hot chips from a stall on the quay, divided them solemnly into two equal heaps and hurried back to the office through the evening, laughing in the cold. For the first time in weeks, and perhaps for the first time in years, Ines was not at all afraid of the future.

That evening, back in the empty office, they pushed their two desks a little closer together and switched on both lamps, which made a warm double circle of light on the maps. Norman the fern sat between them like a small green judge, and the only sounds in the room were the scratch of pencils and, now and then, a soft tune from Jonah. Ines realised that she had not felt so well matched with anyone for years.

First they drew the spine, a long bold line running the whole length of Harbour Road, which was the city's great main street. It had only five large stops, set far apart from one another, so that the express trams could move as fast as even Ines had ever dreamed. For the first time since the contest began, her speed was not in competition with anyone's kindness.

Next Jonah drew the branches, a family of small gentle loops that wandered away from the spine into Lantern Square, Cable Lane and the streets beneath Quay Hill. At every branch stop a tram would wait for a full minute, exactly as he had wanted from the beginning, but because the branches were short, the minutes would never add up into delay. It was a very simple solution, and it had taken two people to see it.

They divided the work without any discussion, as though they had always done it this way: Ines took the timings, the costs and the long columns of numbers, while Jonah took the stops, the riders and the stories behind them. Each of them checked the other's work with the stern kindness of a good editor, and each found, to their surprise, that they were glad to be checked. Tomas, arriving to fetch his scarf, found them at it and left without a word.

At last, at about midnight, it was Ines who solved the problem of Quay Hill, after the longest and most stubborn calculation of the whole night. The depot owned two new light trams with powerful motors and excellent brakes, and these could run up and down the steep street on a short branch of their own, starting from a stop at the foot of the hill. Jonah read her numbers twice, and then he did something quite unexpected, which was to hug her very hard for a moment.

At three in the morning Jonah boiled the office kettle, brewed a strong pot of tea and poured the first cup into his chipped blue mug, which he had never lent to anyone. After a short pause he held it out to Ines instead of drinking it himself, and she took it with both hands, understanding perfectly well what the gesture meant. The tea was very hot and very sweet, and it was, she decided, the best she had ever tasted.

Just before dawn they entered the complete joint timetable into the old Clock, holding their breath, and for once in its long and difficult life the machine accepted every line without a protest. Neither of them trusted it, and so they saved the file in five different places, on two computers, a memory stick and a printed copy, and Jonah put the last one inside his coat. It was partly a joke, but it was also a very sensible precaution after everything the Clock had done to them.

At sunrise they simply ran out of strength and fell asleep in their chairs with their heads resting against the cool window, while the harbour turned from grey to gold in front of them. An hour later they woke, stiff and laughing at their crooked necks, and walked home through the empty streets in the pale morning, parting at the corner of Cable Lane with a shy and mumbled goodbye. Neither of them looked back as they went their separate ways, though both of them very much wanted to.

On Monday morning Mrs Faro found a large map pinned to the wall of the planners' room with two names written at the top, side by side, in two different handwritings. She read it from the first stop to the last without a word, tracing the spine with one finger, and then her stern face broke very slowly into a smile. She told them, quietly, that it was the best piece of planning she had seen in years.

Mrs Faro reminded them gently that the Board would meet on Friday and that, whatever she thought of the plan, there was still officially only one post to be won. Yet she did not tell them to stop, nor to separate their work, and she left the map hanging where it was, which both of them took as the most hopeful sign they were likely to get. For the rest of that week they polished the plan every day, until at last it shone like a new coin.

On Thursday evening, a little after seven, Ines came back to the dim office to fetch the notebook that she had forgotten and stopped dead at the door. Jonah was standing at the far window with his back to her and his phone to his ear, talking in a very low voice that she had never heard him use. She ought to have coughed or called out, and instead she stood perfectly still.

In the quiet of the empty room, every word reached her clearly across the carpet. She heard Jonah say, quite calmly, Yes, Mr Garrity, I will think about your offer, and then, after a pause, I understand that the time is short. Ines took one step backward into the corridor, and the notebook she had come for was entirely forgotten.

She slipped away down the stairs before he could turn, her heart racing so fast that she had to grip the banister. What offer, she asked herself, could the man in the grey suit possibly have made to Jonah, and why on earth would Jonah consider it, after everything that they had built on those nights together? The questions followed her down the stairs, through the glass doors and all the way along the harbour to her flat.

She lay awake all night, and in the darkness the old and familiar fears returned, whispering that she had been foolish to trust anyone and that people who were so very kind were always hiding something. For weeks she had allowed herself to believe otherwise, and now the voice of her old caution told her, with a terrible smugness, that it had been right all along. By the time the grey morning came she had almost convinced herself that she had been right all along.

On Friday, the very day of the Board meeting, Jonah arrived at the office with a cardboard tray holding two coffees and a face full of cheerful hope. He set one cup gently on the corner of her desk and wished her good luck, and Ines looked at it as though it had been a snake and did not say thank you. The people at the nearest desks stopped whatever they were doing, and a little silence began to spread across the floor.

Then she stood up, and before she could stop herself, she told him in a clear and trembling voice, in front of the whole office, that she had heard his telephone call with Mr Garrity. Her pointing finger shook, her face burned, and the planners at their desks fell perfectly silent, each of them staring with the frozen fascination of people who watch a glass fall from a table. Jonah's smile, which had been there since the moment he walked in, went slowly out like a lamp in the wind.

Jonah rose slowly from his seat, holding out both hands, and said in a voice that was quiet but entirely steady that he had turned the offer down. Ines was far too angry to listen, and the more he tried to explain, the louder she spoke, repeating that she had heard it with her own ears and that he had been thinking about it behind her back. She was shouting by now, and she could not seem to stop herself, although a small cold voice inside her kept asking why.

Tomas stared in horror from desk five, Priya half stood with her hand over her mouth, and Mina appeared at the top of the stairs with a ladle in her hand, drawn by the sudden silence. Priya tried to say her friend's name in a low and urgent voice, but Ines, blind with hurt and pride, turned away from her as well. It was a moment that every single person in that room would remember for the rest of their working lives.

Jonah did not shout back, and that was the worst thing of all, because it left her with nothing to push against. He said in a low and level voice that he had honestly believed they were past all this, and then he picked up his chipped blue mug from the desk and walked toward the stairs without another word. The tune he always hummed had stopped, and in the huge silence its absence seemed louder than any noise.

Ines stood alone at her desk for a long moment while the whole office stared at her, and the blood pounded in her ears like a tram going over points. Then, without a word to anyone, she took her coat from the hook and walked down the stairs and out through the glass doors into the cold bright street. She did not know where she was going, only that she could not stay.

Ines walked without thinking until she reached the quay, and there she sat down on a cold iron bench with her coat pulled tight around her. The wind came hard off the water, the gulls wheeled and cried above her head, and the grey sea slapped against the stones as though it too were angry with her. She had never felt so completely alone in the whole of her life, and she had no idea what to do about it.

She told herself, again and again, that she had been right to be careful, that trusting people was a luxury she had never been able to afford, and that it was better to be hurt by suspicion than by hope. But the old argument had lost its force, and it lay in her mind like a coat that no longer fitted. Her stomach was tight with a feeling that she slowly and unwillingly recognised as shame, and it would not go away.

Slowly, in spite of herself, she began to remember the small kindnesses that Jonah had shown her: the printer he had mended, the mistake he had circled so politely and the fern he had moved into the sun. Last of all she remembered the blue mug of tea that he had handed her at three in the morning, which he had never lent to anyone else. A man who had done all that, she realised, was not the kind of man who sold his friends for a salary.

Then somebody sat down on the bench beside her with a small grunt, and a thin, creased hand laid a paper bag of warm buns on the seat between them. He wore a blue cap, he smelled faintly of peppermint, and she knew that cheerful, wrinkled face at once, though she had met it only the one morning. It was Alfie, and he said that he had been looking for her all along the harbour.

Alfie told her, in his slow and gentle voice, that Jonah had come to see him that very morning, white in the face, and told him the whole sad story. The grandson had said no to Mr Garrity, the old man explained, quite clearly and politely on that very telephone call, but Ines had walked out of the room before she could hear the end of it. She closed her eyes and felt the truth land on her like a wave.

The offer, Alfie said, had been a handsome one: a senior post at Garrity and Lowe, a large salary and an office with a view. All Jonah had to do in return was to step aside and let the cheap plan go quietly ahead. It was the kind of offer that would turn most young heads, and Jonah, Alfie said proudly, had needed exactly one minute to refuse it.

Jonah had said no, Alfie told her, because he would never take a job whose price was leaving somebody behind, and he had said it down the telephone in the same stubborn voice that he used for his waiting minute. Then, with his face as red as a ripe tomato, Jonah had added that there was one particular person he had no intention of leaving at all. Ines pressed both hands over her mouth, and for a long moment she could not speak a single word.

She whispered, at last, that she had not even let Jonah finish a sentence, and she said it with such misery that Alfie reached across and patted her hand like a grandfather. A tram waits a minute for anyone who is running, he told her quietly, but it cannot wait for ever, and the Board was due to sit at noon. She looked at her watch and saw that it was nearly a quarter past eleven.

She threw her arms around Alfie, with a hug that nearly knocked the blue cap from his head, and said a thank you that seemed far too small for what he had done. Then she jumped up from the bench and ran back along the quay toward the tram company, her coat flying behind her and her breath coming in great white puffs. Behind her she heard the old man laugh, and say something to the gulls.

Back in the office Ines found desk four completely empty, the chipped blue mug gone from its place and the lamp switched off. On her own desk, squared neatly beside the white cup, lay the finished joint plan, printed and bound, with both of their names on the front cover and hers written first. A little yellow note was stuck to the corner, and she read it standing up.

The note was in Jonah's neat pencil, and it said, in a few plain lines, that he had gone to the Harbour Hall to present the joint plan alone. Her name was first on the cover, it explained, because it ought to be, and she was not obliged to come, though he would keep the second chair empty beside him until the very last minute. At the bottom, in smaller writing and with great care, he had drawn a tiny blue mug beside two small yellow stars.

Ines snatched up the bound plan and her coat and flew toward the stairs, and behind her the whole office seemed to rise at once. Priya shouted good luck, Tomas clapped like a man at a football match, and Mina, from somewhere far below, called something encouraging about soup. Ines took the steps two at a time and did not once look at the clock, because she already knew what it would say.

Outside, the sky had broken open, and a hard cold rain was falling on the street in silvery sheets. The tram for the Harbour Hall was already pulling away from its stop with its lights glowing yellow, and Ines was still half a street behind it. She ran as she had never run before, with the heavy plan in her arms and the water streaming down her neck.

The driver glanced in his mirror and saw a drenched woman sprinting through the rain with a heavy bundle held to her chest, and something in the sight made him stop the tram a hundred metres from the stop. He opened the doors and held them wide, exactly as an old friend of his had done for forty years on Line 9, and he did not close them until she was safely inside. The waiting minute, Ines thought as she dropped into a seat, had arrived at last without anybody having to ask for it.

The driver turned and smiled, and said that an old friend of his called Alfie had telephoned him early that morning. A young woman might come running for this tram, Alfie had said, and he was on no account to leave without her, and Ines laughed and cried at the same moment as she thanked him with her whole heart. It occurred to her that half the city seemed to be quietly working on her behalf.

The tram rolled on through the streaming streets, stopping at each small stop and starting again, while Ines stared at her watch and counted off the minutes. She counted the stops silently under her breath, the way she had counted buses as a girl at the laundry window, and for the first time in her life she wished that a timetable would go faster. Every red signal and every slow passenger seemed to last an hour, and she gripped the plan tighter with each one.

At last the tram drew up before the Harbour Hall, a great grey building with tall doors and a clock tower, and Ines leaped down before the wheels had quite stopped turning. She ran up the wide stone steps two at a time, with rain in her eyes and the plan clutched tightly to her chest, and her wet shoes slapped loudly on the stone. At the top, between two great stone pillars, a young guard stepped forward and held up one hand.

At the great doors a young guard stepped into her path and asked whether she had an appointment, and Ines, gasping, gave her name and explained that she was the other planner and that the Board was waiting for her. He looked at her dripping hair, her ruined shoes and her fierce face, and then he smiled, stepped aside and pushed open the tall doors for her. She never learned his name, though she would always remember the kindness of that young man in the doorway.

Inside the hall a tall, lonely figure stood before the long table of the Board, speaking in a steady voice, with a single empty chair waiting at his side. Behind him on the great screen glowed Mr Garrity's cheap and tidy plan, and Jonah was in the middle of explaining, with great politeness and no bitterness whatever, why a city needed more than a bargain. His chipped blue mug, the one thing in the great room that looked at all homely, sat on the table beside his elbow.

At that moment the tall door opened behind him, and Ines walked into the great hall, dripping and breathless, and made her way down the long aisle to the empty chair beside Jonah's. He turned his head and saw her, and his whole face lit up like a lamp in a dark window, so brightly that several members of the Board smiled. She sat down beside him and laid the bound plan on the table between them, where everyone could see both of their names.

Dripping and breathless, Ines rose to her feet beside Jonah and, with a steadiness that astonished her, began to present the joint plan to the Board. She explained the timings, the costs and the long fast spine along Harbour Road, and he took up the story at each branch and described the people who would stand at its stops. They had not rehearsed a single word of it, and yet they never once interrupted each other or lost the thread.

Mr Garrity rose with a thin smile and declared that the joint plan was sentimental, soft and far too expensive for a sensible city. Ines answered him number by number, quietly and without a single note, and she showed that the fast spine and short branches would cost less in the long run. His own plan, she added, would lose riders and need to be rebuilt, and by the end he had stopped smiling altogether.

Mrs Adeyemi, the nurse, leaned forward and asked quietly what the waiting minute would really mean for a tired person running home after a night shift. Jonah answered that on every branch a tram would wait for one whole minute for anyone running toward it, and that the spine would make up the time so that nobody else lost anything. She sat back and smiled, and she wrote nothing at all in her notebook, because, as she said later, she had heard everything that she needed.

While the Board debated behind closed doors, the two planners waited side by side on a stone bench in the corridor, drying slowly in the draught. Ines said, in a very small voice, that she was sorry, and that she should have let him finish, and Jonah answered, with a smile, that the tram had still been running and she had caught it. He took her cold hand in both of his and held it there, without a word, until the great doors opened again.

At last the doors opened and the Board filed back to their seats, and Mr Hale, who had said nothing all morning, rose slowly and cleared his throat. He told the hall that the members had agreed, after careful thought, that they preferred the joint plan of Ines Marlow and Jonah Pike to the plan of the consultants. A great round of applause broke out among the staff crowded at the back, and Mr Garrity quietly gathered his papers and slipped out of the hall without a word.

Mrs Faro stood up beside Mr Hale with a pair of cream envelopes in her hands and the broadest smile that anyone in the company had ever seen on her face. She announced that the Board had decided that a line so large deserved two Heads of Planning, one fast and one gentle, and that their names were Ines Marlow and Jonah Pike. Ines turned to Jonah, who was already staring at her with his mouth open, and then she threw her arms around him while Priya, Mina and Tomas cheered from the back.

A few weeks later the first test tram of Line 12 rolled out of Seagate Depot, and the company, with great ceremony, had asked old Alfie to drive it. At a stop on Gull Street a young woman with a baby came hurrying down the pavement, and Alfie held the doors open for the whole of the minute. In that minute, with the golden light on the harbour and the old man pretending not to look, Ines and Jonah kissed, and Alfie rang the brass bell twice, loudly, and then muttered something about the timetable.

The next morning, on a sudden impulse, Ines bought a bright yellow mug from the little shop at the depot, the cheerful colour of the old Line 9 trams and nothing at all like her usual plain white cup. Jonah looked at it for a long moment and said that he had never seen a lovelier thing, and that it would look wonderful next to a blue one with a chip. She carried it back to the office as carefully as if it were made of gold.

Six months later the first public Line 12 tram rolled out of the depot exactly on time, its fast spine gleaming and its branches humming, with a small crowd waving along Harbour Road. At the first branch stop the driver paused, as the plan promised, for a young girl who came pounding up the street with her school bag bouncing on her back. The doors did not close until she was safely aboard, and so nobody on that first tram, not one single person, had been left behind.

Back at the office, desks three and four had been pushed together beneath the big window to make a single island, where Norman the fern grew greener than ever between two lamps. Jonah's chipped blue mug now sat beside Ines's cheerful new yellow one, and the two of them hummed the same wandering tune, one a little flat and one a little sharp. The rival at desk four had become the person that she most wanted to see every morning.
